South American dishes.Ceviche: Raw fish is 'cooked' in lime juice, whose acid firms up the flesh; it is Peru's national dish and has its own holiday there.
South American dishes.Arepa: Griddled cornmeal cakes eaten daily in Venezuela and Colombia, split open and stuffed like a sandwich.
South American dishes.Feijoada: Brazil's black bean stew with pork cuts is traditionally served on Saturdays with rice, greens and orange slices.
South American dishes.Chimichurri: Argentina's green sauce of parsley, garlic, oregano and vinegar is the classic partner for grilled steak.
South American dishes.Asado: More a social ritual than a dish, this slow barbecue of beef cuts over embers is central to Argentine and Uruguayan weekends.
South American dishes.Pão de queijo: These Brazilian cheese breads from Minas Gerais are chewy and naturally gluten-free because they're made with tapioca flour.
South American dishes.Brigadeiro: Brazil's fudgy chocolate truffle of condensed milk and cocoa is named after a 1940s air force brigadier who ran for president.
South American dishes.Lomo saltado: A Peruvian stir-fry of beef, onions and tomatoes served with fries and rice, showing the influence of Chinese immigrants' wok cooking.
South American dishes.Churrasco: Brazilian-style grilled meat, often carved at the table from big skewers in steakhouses called churrascarias.
South American dishes.Anticuchos: Peruvian skewers of marinated beef heart, grilled street-side; the tradition goes back to the Inca era.
South American dishes.Alfajores: Two crumbly cookies sandwiching dulce de leche, a treat across South America; the name comes from Arabic, via Spain.
South American dishes.Coxinha: Brazil's teardrop-shaped, breaded and fried chicken croquette is a favorite party snack across the country.
South American dishes.Açaí bowl: The Amazon berry blended into a thick, icy purée is eaten in Brazil as a energy food, often with granola and banana.
South American dishes.Tacos: Mexico's tortilla-wrapped classic comes from North America, not South America, though they're now eaten worldwide.
South American dishes.Enchiladas: Rolled, sauce-covered tortillas are a Mexican creation, so this North American dish doesn't belong here.
South American dishes.Pupusa: Although it is Latin American, this stuffed corn tortilla is the national dish of El Salvador, in Central America.
South American dishes.Mole: Mexico's famously complex sauce can include dozens of ingredients, even chocolate, and the Oaxacan and Pueblan versions are celebrated.
South American dishes.Jerk chicken: Jamaican barbecue marinated with allspice and fiery Scotch bonnet pepper; it belongs to the Caribbean.
South American dishes.Gumbo: This thick Louisiana stew is rooted in the American South, not South America.
South American dishes.Mofongo: Puerto Rico's mashed fried plantain dish is Caribbean, not South American, even if the idea is shared across Latin America.
South American dishes.Pozole: A hominy stew from Mexico that goes back to Aztec times, so it's North American.
South American dishes.Burrito: The name means 'little donkey' in Spanish, but this wrapped tortilla is a northern Mexican and Tex-Mex invention.
South American dishes.Quesadilla: A cheese-filled tortilla, folded and toasted, this is a Mexican dish, not South American.
South American dishes.Chilaquiles: Fried tortilla chips simmered in salsa and served at breakfast are a Mexican hangover cure, not South American.

Actual bears.Grizzly bear: A grizzly is a North American brown bear, and its name comes from the silvery 'grizzled' tips of its fur.
Actual bears.Polar bear: Polar bears have black skin under translucent, hollow fur, and they can smell a seal from over a kilometre away.
Actual bears.Giant panda: Giant pandas are true bears, and they eat bamboo for up to 14 hours a day despite having a carnivore's gut.
Actual bears.Sloth bear: The sloth bear has no upper front teeth, so it sucks up termites like a vacuum and even carries its cubs on its back.
Actual bears.Sun bear: The smallest bear, the sun bear has a very long tongue and a pale chest patch said to resemble a rising sun.
Actual bears.Black bear: American black bears aren't always black; some are cinnamon, blond, or, in a rare coastal form, creamy white.
Actual bears.Spectacled bear: The only bear native to South America, it's named for pale rings around its eyes, which vary from one bear to the next.
Actual bears.Kodiak bear: A bearded dragon is an Australian lizard; its 'beard' is a spiny throat pouch that puffs out when it feels threatened.
Actual bears.Brown bear: The most widespread bear, the brown bear ranges across North America, Europe and Asia, and hibernates for months in winter.
Actual bears.Koala: Koalas are marsupials, not bears; they sleep around 20 hours a day to cope with a low-energy eucalyptus diet.
Actual bears.Red panda: The red panda is not a bear but belongs to its own family, and it eats mostly bamboo like the giant panda.
Actual bears.Wolverine: A wolverine is the largest land-dwelling member of the weasel family, so it's a bear lookalike in strength only.
Actual bears.Raccoon: Raccoons are not bears; they're in a separate family, and their dexterous front paws can open jars and latches.
Actual bears.Binturong: This Southeast Asian animal, also called a bearcat, is a relative of civets and smells like buttered popcorn.
Actual bears.Water bear: Water bears, or tardigrades, are microscopic animals that can survive space vacuum, radiation and years without water.
Actual bears.Bearded dragon: A bearded dragon is a lizard from Australia; its 'beard' is a throat pouch that puffs up when it feels threatened.
Actual bears.Anteater: Wombats are marsupials, not bears, and they're the only animals known to produce cube-shaped droppings.
Actual bears.Wombat: Anteaters aren't related to bears; a giant anteater's sticky tongue is about 60 cm long and flicks in and out roughly 150 times a minute.
Actual bears.Badger: Badgers belong to the weasel family, not the bear family, and they live in large underground burrow systems called setts.
Actual bears.Sea lion: Sea lions are eared seals, not bears, although both belong to the same wider group of carnivores, the caniforms.
Actual bears.Woolly bear: The woolly bear is a caterpillar, the larva of the Isabella tiger moth; folklore says its stripes predict winter severity, but science disagrees.
Actual bears.Honey badger: The honey badger is a weasel relative famous for fearlessly attacking beehives and snakes, not a bear at all.
Actual bears.Gummy bear: Gummy bears were invented in Germany in the 1920s by Hans Riegel, founder of Haribo, and have nothing to do with real bears.
Actual bears.Bear cat: The binturong is called a bearcat, but it's neither: it's a civet relative with a prehensile tail.

Insects that can fly.Bee: A honeybee flaps its wings about 230 times a second, and that is what makes the buzz.
Insects that can fly.Wasp: Though often thought of as pests, wasps are skilled pollinators and also hunt pest insects.
Insects that can fly.Dragonfly: A dragonfly can fly in any direction, including backward, and catches about 95 percent of the prey it chases.
Insects that can fly.Butterfly: Monarch butterflies migrate up to 4,000 kilometers to Mexico, a place none of the migrating individuals has seen before.
Insects that can fly.Moth: Moths navigate by moonlight, and artificial lights confuse them into spiraling in.
Insects that can fly.Housefly: A housefly beats its wings about 200 times per second, and it tastes with its feet.
Insects that can fly.Mosquito: Only the females bite, because they need blood protein to make eggs, and their wings beat hundreds of times a second.
Insects that can fly.Ladybug: Ladybugs tuck delicate flying wings under their hard red wing covers, and they can fly high in the air.
Insects that can fly.Firefly: It's actually a beetle, and its flashes are a courtship code, made by a chemical reaction nearly without heat.
Insects that can fly.Cicada: Some cicadas fly after spending 13 or 17 years underground, then emerge together in the millions.
Insects that can fly.Locust: Locusts are grasshoppers that swarm; a swarm can contain billions of insects and travel 150 kilometers in a day.
Insects that can fly.Hornet: Hornets are large social wasps, and some species can fly for long distances and fiercely defend their nests.
Insects that can fly.Flea: A trap: fleas have no wings, but their leaps can reach about 100 times their body length.
Insects that can fly.Silverfish: A wingless, ancient insect that has barely changed in hundreds of millions of years, and it never flies.
Insects that can fly.Head louse: A trap: lice have no wings and cling to hair with tiny claws, spreading only by contact.
Insects that can fly.Worker ant: A trap: most ants walk their whole lives. Only young queens and males grow wings, for the mating flight.
Insects that can fly.Bed bug: Wingless, bed bugs move only by crawling, but they can survive months without a meal.
Insects that can fly.Spider: A trap: spiders aren't insects, since they have eight legs, and none has wings, though young ones can balloon on silk threads.
Insects that can fly.Centipede: Not an insect at all, and wingless, with a pair of legs on each body segment.
Insects that can fly.Tick: Ticks are arachnids rather than insects, and they cannot fly or jump; they climb on grass and wait.
Insects that can fly.Woodlouse: A crustacean, closer to crabs than insects, and wingless; it breathes with gill-like structures.
Insects that can fly.Scorpion: An arachnid without wings, famous for glowing under ultraviolet light.
Insects that can fly.Mite: Tiny arachnids that cannot fly, among the most abundant animals on Earth.
Insects that can fly.Caterpillar: A trap: it's the larval stage, and it has no wings, but it will become a flier after turning into a moth or butterfly.

Squashes.Butternut: Its sweet, nutty flesh deepens in flavor with storage, and it has a bulbous bottom holding seeds.
Squashes.Acorn squash: Its name comes from the shape, a ribbed, acorn-like fruit with dark green skin.
Squashes.Spaghetti squash: The cooked flesh pulls apart into strands that resemble spaghetti, a popular low-carb swap.
Squashes.Pumpkin: Canned 'pumpkin' for pie is often a different squash variety, as pumpkins and squash are the same species group.
Squashes.Zucchini: A courgette in Britain, picked unripe, and you can eat its blossoms too.
Squashes.Kabocha: The Japanese squash is sweet and dense, with a name believed to derive from the Portuguese word for Cambodia.
Squashes.Delicata: The skin is thin enough to eat, so there's no peeling, and it is sweet.
Squashes.Pattypan: Also called scallop squash, it looks like a flying saucer, and is eaten young.
Squashes.Hubbard: Its thick, bumpy shell is so hard that cooks sometimes crack it open with a hammer.
Squashes.Crookneck: Named for the curved neck, this yellow summer squash has bumpy skin.
Squashes.Turban squash: A turban-shaped squash with a cap, often used as decoration, though edible.
Squashes.Cucumber: Same family as squash, but a separate genus, Cucumis, and 95 percent water.
Squashes.Watermelon: Same gourd family as squash, but a separate genus, Citrullus, and originated in Africa.
Squashes.Cantaloupe: A melon in the same family as squash, though its genus is Cucumis, and it has a netted rind.
Squashes.Eggplant: A nightshade related to tomatoes and potatoes, not squash, and technically a berry.
Squashes.Sweet potato: Not a squash. It's a root crop, related to morning glories, and sweeter than the true yam.
Squashes.Yam: True yams are unrelated plants, from Africa and Asia, so not squash.
Squashes.Okra: A mallow relative, that is related to hibiscus and cotton, not squash, and its pods get slimy.
Squashes.Bell pepper: A nightshade fruit, so not squash, and the green ones are simply unripe.
Squashes.Jicama: A Mexican root vegetable that is crisp and watery, a legume relative, and not a squash.
Squashes.Parsnip: A root related to carrots, so not a squash, and sweeter after frost.
Squashes.Kohlrabi: The stem swells into a bulb, a cabbage relative, not squash. Its name means cabbage-turnip in German.
Squashes.Turnip: A root vegetable of the cabbage family, not a squash, with both greens and roots edible.
Squashes.Celeriac: A knobby celery relative, so not a squash, with a root that tastes of celery.

Dishes served uncooked.Sashimi: Sliced raw fish served without rice. In Japan it is traditionally the first course of a formal meal.
Dishes served uncooked.Steak tartare: Raw minced beef with egg yolk and capers. Its name is said to come from Tatar horsemen, but that is a legend.
Dishes served uncooked.Carpaccio: Paper-thin raw beef, created at Harry's Bar in Venice in 1950 and named for the painter Vittore Carpaccio.
Dishes served uncooked.Gazpacho: Spanish cold soup of raw blended vegetables. It predates tomatoes in Europe, when it was made with bread, garlic and oil.
Dishes served uncooked.Guacamole: Mashed avocado with lime and salt. The name comes from Nahuatl, ahuacamolli, which means avocado sauce.
Dishes served uncooked.Coleslaw: Raw shredded cabbage in dressing. The name comes from the Dutch koolsla, meaning cabbage salad.
Dishes served uncooked.Caprese salad: Tomato, mozzarella and basil from Capri, matching the Italian flag. The island lent its name.
Dishes served uncooked.Poke: Hawaiian raw fish salad whose name means to slice or cut. Cubed ahi tuna with soy and sesame is the classic.
Dishes served uncooked.Pico de gallo: Fresh chopped tomato, onion, chili and lime. Its name means rooster's beak in Spanish.
Dishes served uncooked.Crudités: French for raw things, an array of vegetables served with dip. The word sums up the whole dish.
Dishes served uncooked.Smoothie: Blended raw fruit, often with yogurt or milk. The name took off in the 1960s with health food stores.
Dishes served uncooked.Fruit salad: A mix of raw cut fruit. Pineapple and kiwi contain enzymes that break down gelatin, so they ruin jellies.
Dishes served uncooked.Risotto: Rice cooked in stock for about 20 minutes. Stirring releases the starch for its creamy finish.
Dishes served uncooked.French toast: Bread soaked in egg, then fried. The egg must be cooked through.
Dishes served uncooked.Soufflé: Baked egg dish that puffs up in the oven. It collapses quickly after leaving it.
Dishes served uncooked.Meatloaf: Ground meat baked in a loaf pan. It needs to reach 71 C inside to be safe.
Dishes served uncooked.Paella: Spanish rice cooked over an open flame in a wide pan. The pan, called paellera, gives the dish its name.
Dishes served uncooked.Pho: Beef noodle soup with a broth simmered for hours. Thin raw beef slices are cooked by the hot broth when served.
Dishes served uncooked.Pot roast: Tough cuts of beef braised slowly until tender. Long, moist cooking breaks down collagen into gelatin.
Dishes served uncooked.Ratatouille: Provencal vegetable stew of eggplant, zucchini, peppers and tomato, all cooked. The dish became an animated film in 2007.
Dishes served uncooked.Lasagne: Layered pasta baked with sauce and cheese. Its name probably comes from the Greek word for cooking pot.
Dishes served uncooked.Shakshuka: Eggs poached in spicy tomato sauce, popular across North Africa and Israel. The word is Arabic for mixed.
Dishes served uncooked.Biryani: Rice and meat layered and cooked slowly. It's a dish from Mughal kitchens.
Dishes served uncooked.Tempura: Battered and deep-fried. Cooking takes mere minutes at high heat.

Foods usually eaten cold.Gazpacho: A chilled soup from Andalusia, served cold in summer. Before tomatoes arrived from the Americas it was made with bread, garlic and oil.
Foods usually eaten cold.Vichyssoise: Chilled leek and potato soup. It was served cold by Ritz-Carlton's chef Louis Diat in New York in 1917, who gave it a French name.
Foods usually eaten cold.Ice cream: Frozen sweet cream. Brain freeze happens when cold hits the palate and sends a message that triggers a headache.
Foods usually eaten cold.Sorbet: A frozen dessert of fruit and sugar without dairy. Its name traces back to the Turkish and Arabic word for a cold drink.
Foods usually eaten cold.Gelato: Italian ice cream with less air and less fat, which makes it denser. It is served slightly warmer than ice cream.
Foods usually eaten cold.Potato salad: Potatoes dressed with mayonnaise or vinaigrette. German versions are often served warm with bacon.
Foods usually eaten cold.Panna cotta: Italian for cooked cream, a set dessert that has to chill before serving. Gelatin gives it a gentle wobble.
Foods usually eaten cold.Popsicle: Invented by 11-year-old Frank Epperson in 1905, who left a soda with a stick outside overnight.
Foods usually eaten cold.Granita: A Sicilian frozen dessert of ice crystals, often eaten with a brioche for breakfast in summer.
Foods usually eaten cold.Iced tea: Became popular at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair when a heatwave made hot tea unsellable, according to legend.
Foods usually eaten cold.Cheesecake: Chilled to set in the fridge. New York style versions are baked first, but all are served cold.
Foods usually eaten cold.Sashimi: Raw fish served chilled. The fish must stay cold to keep it fresh and safe.
Foods usually eaten cold.Tiramisu: Italian for pick me up, a chilled dessert of coffee-soaked ladyfingers and mascarpone, created in the Veneto in the 1960s or 1970s.
Foods usually eaten cold.Ramen: Hot noodle soup, though there are cold ramen dishes in summer, called hiyashi chuka.
Foods usually eaten cold.Pho: Vietnamese soup that must arrive scalding. Raw beef cooks in the broth at the table.
Foods usually eaten cold.Fondue: Melted cheese in a pot kept warm over a flame. Dropping bread in your pot is, by tradition, a reason for forfeits.
Foods usually eaten cold.Mulled wine: Wine heated with spices like cloves and cinnamon. It is a winter drink in northern Europe.
Foods usually eaten cold.Hot chocolate: Served steaming. In Spain it can be thick enough to dip churros in.
Foods usually eaten cold.Lasagne: Baked pasta served hot. Many say it tastes better the day after, but it is reheated.
Foods usually eaten cold.Soufflé: Needs to be served the moment it leaves the oven, since it deflates as it cools.
Foods usually eaten cold.French onion soup: Served bubbling hot, topped with melted cheese on bread. The onions are caramelized for ages.
Foods usually eaten cold.Baked potato: Eaten hot with butter. Wrapping it in foil actually steams it rather than baking.
Foods usually eaten cold.Hot toddy: A warm mix of whisky, honey, lemon and hot water. Popular as a folk remedy for colds.
Foods usually eaten cold.Grilled cheese: A hot sandwich of melted cheese in toasted bread. Cold, the cheese goes rubbery.

Islands in the Indian Ocean.Madagascar: The world's fourth-largest island, Madagascar has lemurs found nowhere else, and it split from Africa about 160 million years ago.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Sri Lanka: The teardrop-shaped island was called Ceylon until 1972, and its tea has made it famous.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Maldives: The lowest country on Earth, the Maldives average about 1.5 meters above sea level, so rising seas threaten them.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Mauritius: Mauritius is the former home of the dodo, a flightless bird driven extinct in the 1600s.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Seychelles: The Seychelles hold the coco de mer, a palm whose seed is the largest in the plant kingdom, weighing up to 25 kg.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Zanzibar: Zanzibar was a major spice and trade hub, and Freddie Mercury was born here.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Réunion: Réunion is a French island with one of the world's most active volcanoes, Piton de la Fournaise.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Comoros: The Comoros is a volcanic archipelago between Africa and Madagascar, and the coelacanth, a living fossil fish, was found nearby.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Andaman Islands: The Andamans are an Indian archipelago, home to the Sentinelese, who reject all contact with outsiders.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Socotra: Socotra's dragon blood trees look like upside-down umbrellas, and a third of its plants are found nowhere else.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Fiji: Fiji lies in the Pacific Ocean, thousands of kilometers from the Indian Ocean.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Tahiti: Tahiti is in the Pacific, and is part of French Polynesia.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Bermuda: Bermuda is in the Atlantic Ocean, with a subtropical climate warmed by the Gulf Stream.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Cuba: Cuba is in the Caribbean, which belongs to the Atlantic, not the Indian Ocean.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Hawaii: Hawaii sits in the middle of the Pacific, about 3,900 km from California.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Sicily: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean, and its volcano, Mount Etna, is among Europe's most active.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Galápagos: The Galápagos are in the Pacific off Ecuador, and are where Darwin studied finches.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Iceland: Iceland is in the North Atlantic, with glaciers and volcanoes sharing the same island.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Samoa: Samoa is in the Pacific, and skipped a day in 2011 by shifting across the date line.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Jamaica: Jamaica is in the Caribbean Sea, an arm of the Atlantic, not the Indian Ocean.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Malta: Malta is in the Mediterranean, and one of the most densely populated countries in the world.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Crete: Crete is a Mediterranean island and the site of the Minoan civilization, one of Europe's oldest.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Easter Island: Easter Island is in the Pacific, one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth.
Islands in the Indian Ocean.Bahamas: The Bahamas are in the Atlantic, off Florida, so not an Indian Ocean island group.

Currencies used in Asia.Yen: Japan's currency means round, and it is the third most traded currency in the world.
Currencies used in Asia.Yuan: China's currency is formally the renminbi, meaning people's currency, and yuan is its unit.
Currencies used in Asia.Won: South Korea and North Korea both use a won, and it shares its character with the yuan and the yen, all meaning round.
Currencies used in Asia.Rupee: The word comes from Sanskrit for silver, and it is used in India, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and elsewhere.
Currencies used in Asia.Baht: Thailand's baht started out as a unit of weight, used for measuring silver.
Currencies used in Asia.Ringgit: Malaysia's currency means jagged, after the milled edges of old Spanish silver dollars.
Currencies used in Asia.Dong: Vietnam's dong has very large numbers: the 500,000 dong note is worth only about 20 US dollars.
Currencies used in Asia.Rupiah: Indonesia's currency also comes from the rupee, and its banknotes can run into millions.
Currencies used in Asia.Riel: Cambodia's riel exists beside the US dollar, which is widely used in daily life there.
Currencies used in Asia.Kip: Laos uses the kip, and banknotes hold big denominations for small purchases.
Currencies used in Asia.Taka: Bangladesh's taka comes from the Sanskrit tanka, and it is written with a distinctive Bengali symbol.
Currencies used in Asia.Euro: A trap. The euro is used in about 20 European countries, not in Asia.
Currencies used in Asia.Rand: South Africa's rand is named for the Witwatersrand gold fields, not for an Asian country.
Currencies used in Asia.Real: Brazil's real is South American, and the word is Portuguese for royal.
Currencies used in Asia.Krona: Sweden's currency means crown, as does the related Danish and Norwegian krone.
Currencies used in Asia.Zloty: Poland's zloty means golden, and it is European.
Currencies used in Asia.Forint: Hungary's forint is named after the Florentine florin, a famous medieval gold coin.
Currencies used in Asia.Naira: Nigeria's naira replaced the pound in 1973, and it is African, not Asian.
Currencies used in Asia.Kwacha: Zambia and Malawi's currency, the word means dawn in local languages, for the dawn of independence.
Currencies used in Asia.Cedi: Ghana's cedi is named after the cowrie shell, once used as money in West Africa.
Currencies used in Asia.Bolivar: Venezuela's old currency honors Simón Bolívar, South America's liberator.
Currencies used in Asia.Koruna: The Czech koruna and Slovakia's former currency both mean crown.
Currencies used in Asia.Leu: Romania's leu means lion, and it is the currency of an EU member outside the eurozone.
Currencies used in Asia.Franc: Switzerland and many African countries use francs, names from the Latin Francorum Rex.

Cities in Texas.Houston: Named for Sam Houston, the hero of the Texas Revolution, it is home to NASA's Johnson Space Center, where mission control says 'Houston' to astronauts.
Cities in Texas.Dallas: President Kennedy was assassinated here in 1963, and the city also gave the world the TV show Dallas and the Cowboys.
Cities in Texas.Austin: The state capital calls itself the Live Music Capital of the World, and it hosts the huge South by Southwest festival.
Cities in Texas.San Antonio: The Alamo is here, and its River Walk is a network of paths below street level lined with restaurants.
Cities in Texas.El Paso: Sitting in the far west corner of Texas, it is closer to California's capital than to Houston, and it is in the Mountain Time Zone.
Cities in Texas.Fort Worth: Cowtown's stockyards still run a twice-daily cattle drive, and the city is famous for the Kimbell Art Museum.
Cities in Texas.Corpus Christi: Named in Latin for the 'Body of Christ', it is a Gulf port with some of the longest undeveloped barrier-island beaches in the US nearby.
Cities in Texas.Lubbock: Rock pioneer Buddy Holly was born in this West Texas city on the flat Llano Estacado, and it is known for its cotton fields.
Cities in Texas.Amarillo: Its name is Spanish for yellow, and it is home to Cadillac Ranch, a row of cars buried nose-down in a field.
Cities in Texas.Waco: The home of Dr Pepper, invented here in 1885, plus Baylor University and the Magnolia home-design empire.
Cities in Texas.Galveston: In 1900 a hurricane killed thousands here in the deadliest natural disaster in US history, after which the entire city was raised several feet.
Cities in Texas.Oklahoma City: Trap: the capital of Oklahoma, just across the Red River from Texas, is not in the Lone Star State.
Cities in Texas.Tulsa: Trap: this Oklahoma city once called itself the Oil Capital of the World and has rich Art Deco architecture.
Cities in Texas.Phoenix: Trap: Arizona's capital is one of the hottest big cities in the country and not in Texas.
Cities in Texas.Albuquerque: Trap: New Mexico's biggest city, and the setting of the TV show Breaking Bad, lies just west of the Texas border.
Cities in Texas.New Orleans: Trap: the Louisiana city is known for Mardi Gras and jazz, and it sits on the Mississippi near the Gulf, east of Texas.
Cities in Texas.Baton Rouge: Trap: Louisiana's capital, whose name is French for red stick, referring to a marker pole between native hunting grounds.
Cities in Texas.Santa Fe: Trap: New Mexico's capital has Spanish roots like many Texas towns, but it belongs to the state to the west.
Cities in Texas.Little Rock: Trap: Arkansas's capital, named for a small rock outcrop on the Arkansas River, and famous for the 1957 school integration crisis.
Cities in Texas.Denver: Trap: the Mile High City is Colorado's capital, about 5,280 feet up, and nowhere near Texas.
Cities in Texas.Monterrey: Trap: it sounds like a Texas town but is a Mexican city in Nuevo Leon, about 140 miles south of the border.
Cities in Texas.Tucson: Trap: this Arizona city boasts the Saguaro cactus in its national park, and sits well west of Texas.
Cities in Texas.Shreveport: Trap: a Louisiana city near the Texas line, named for Captain Henry Shreve, who cleared the Red River's huge log jam.
Cities in Texas.Wichita: Trap: Kansas's biggest city is called the Air Capital of the World because many US aircraft makers started here.

Places in the Czech Republic.Prague: The Czech capital's astronomical clock has told time since 1410 and is the oldest still working, and its castle complex is among the largest in the world.
Places in the Czech Republic.Brno: The country's second city, where Gregor Mendel, the father of genetics, studied peas in a monastery garden.
Places in the Czech Republic.Charles Bridge: Begun in 1357, legend says egg yolks were mixed into the mortar to strengthen it; Baroque statues line its length.
Places in the Czech Republic.Český Krumlov: A fairy-tale town curled in a river bend, with a castle that has a rotating open-air theater.
Places in the Czech Republic.Karlovy Vary: A spa town famed for hot mineral springs, and for a film festival and herbal liqueur Becherovka.
Places in the Czech Republic.Pilsen: The birthplace of pilsner beer in 1842, the original golden lager, whose name inspired countless imitations.
Places in the Czech Republic.Kutná Hora: A medieval silver-mining town whose Sedlec Ossuary church is decorated with the bones of tens of thousands of people.
Places in the Czech Republic.Ostrava: A former coal and steel city, now reborn with an industrial-heritage site at Lower Vítkovice.
Places in the Czech Republic.Olomouc: A university city with a Holy Trinity Column, a World Heritage site, and a quirky local cheese.
Places in the Czech Republic.Prague Castle: The largest ancient castle complex in the world, according to Guinness, and it is the seat of the president.
Places in the Czech Republic.Kraków: A Polish city whose Wawel Castle and old town draw visitors, in Poland, not the Czech Republic.
Places in the Czech Republic.Wrocław: A Polish city of bridges, famous for hundreds of tiny gnome statues.
Places in the Czech Republic.Gdańsk: A Baltic port in Poland, where the Solidarity movement was born in 1980.
Places in the Czech Republic.Bratislava: The capital of Slovakia, once part of Czechoslovakia with Prague and now independent.
Places in the Czech Republic.Vienna: The Austrian capital is known for coffeehouses and imperial palaces, and lies only a short drive from Czech borders.
Places in the Czech Republic.Budapest: The Hungarian capital is divided by the Danube into hilly Buda and flat Pest, which were joined in 1873.
Places in the Czech Republic.Dresden: A German city on the Elbe, rebuilt after 1945, noted for the Frauenkirche.
Places in the Czech Republic.Salzburg: Mozart's Austrian birthplace and the setting of The Sound of Music, so it lies in Austria, not in the Czech Republic.
Places in the Czech Republic.Ljubljana: The capital of Slovenia, with dragon-topped bridges and a car-free old center, a neighbor of Austria and Italy.
Places in the Czech Republic.Zakopane: A Polish mountain resort town in the Tatras, popular for skiing and for its wooden highlander architecture.
Places in the Czech Republic.Košice: Slovakia's second city, a European Capital of Culture in 2013, with the largest Gothic cathedral in the country.
Places in the Czech Republic.Lake Balaton: The largest lake in Central Europe, in Hungary, nicknamed the Hungarian sea.
Places in the Czech Republic.Wawel Castle: A royal castle on a hill in Kraków, Poland, once home to Polish kings, and not in Prague.
Places in the Czech Republic.Debrecen: Hungary's second-largest city, a long-time center of Calvinism, nicknamed the Calvinist Rome, located in the east.

National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Canberra: Australia's purpose-built capital was a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne, designed by American architect Walter Burley Griffin.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Wellington: The world's southernmost capital of a sovereign state, and well known for its wind.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Buenos Aires: South America's tango capital sits at about 34 degrees south, on the Rio de la Plata.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Santiago: Chile's capital lies in a valley with the snowy Andes rising right behind it.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Lima: The Peruvian capital sits at around 12 degrees south, a desert city that gets almost no rain.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Pretoria: It is the executive capital of South Africa, which unusually has three capitals, and it is known for jacaranda trees.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Nairobi: Just 1 degree south of the equator, it has a national park within the city limits where lions roam.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Jakarta: At about 6 degrees south, it is sinking so fast that Indonesia is moving its capital to Nusantara on Borneo.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Brasília: Built from scratch in the late 1950s and inaugurated in 1960, it was designed in the shape of an airplane.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Montevideo: The capital of Uruguay, home to nearly half the country's population, lies on the southern bank of the Rio de la Plata.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Antananarivo: The capital of Madagascar sits high in the central highlands and its name means city of the thousand.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Luanda: Angola's capital is on the Atlantic coast and is one of the most expensive cities in the world for expatriates.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Harare: The capital of Zimbabwe, at about 18 degrees south, was once named Salisbury.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Bogotá: Despite being in South America, it lies north of the equator at about 4 degrees north.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Caracas: Venezuela's capital is at about 10 degrees north, firmly in the Northern Hemisphere.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Singapore: Only about 1 degree north of the equator, so it is in the Northern Hemisphere, if barely.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Kuala Lumpur: At roughly 3 degrees north, it is near the equator but still north of it.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Addis Ababa: At about 9 degrees north and 2,355 metres high, it is one of the highest capitals in the world.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Abuja: Nigeria's purpose-built capital replaced Lagos in 1991, and lies at 9 degrees north.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Accra: Ghana's capital is about 5 degrees north, just above the equator.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Manila: Philippine capital at about 14 degrees north, well into the Northern Hemisphere.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Bangkok: At about 14 degrees north, with the longest official place name of any capital in the world.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Panama City: At about 9 degrees north, it sits at the Pacific end of the Panama Canal.
National capitals in the Southern Hemisp.Mogadishu: Somalia's capital is at about 2 degrees north, a hair's breadth above the equator.

Landmarks in South America.Machu Picchu: The Inca citadel in Peru, built in the 1400s high in the Andes, was unknown to the outside world until Hiram Bingham made it famous in 1911.
Landmarks in South America.Christ the Redeemer: The statue above Rio de Janeiro is about 30 meters tall with arms stretching 28 meters, and it was finished in 1931.
Landmarks in South America.Iguazu Falls: On the border of Argentina and Brazil, it has about 275 separate drops, and its Devil's Throat is the most powerful.
Landmarks in South America.Angel Falls: Venezuela's cascade drops almost 1,000 meters, making it the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall.
Landmarks in South America.Galápagos: The islands off Ecuador inspired Darwin's ideas, and many species there found nowhere else evolved on separate islands.
Landmarks in South America.Salar de Uyuni: Bolivia's salt flat is the largest in the world, and in the wet season it becomes a vast mirror of sky.
Landmarks in South America.Torres del Paine: A Chilean national park in Patagonia named for three granite spires, famed for its W trek.
Landmarks in South America.Lake Titicaca: Straddling Peru and Bolivia at about 3,800 meters, it is one of the highest navigable lakes and has islands made of reeds.
Landmarks in South America.Sugarloaf Mountain: A granite peak in Rio de Janeiro, reached by a cable car that has run since 1912.
Landmarks in South America.Atacama Desert: In Chile, it is the driest non-polar desert, and some weather stations there have recorded no rain for years.
Landmarks in South America.Aconcagua: At about 6,960 meters in Argentina, it is the tallest mountain outside Asia.
Landmarks in South America.Patagonia: A vast region at the tip of South America shared by Argentina and Chile, with glaciers and steppe.
Landmarks in South America.Chichen Itza: This Maya city in Mexico has the El Castillo pyramid, and it is in North America, not South America.
Landmarks in South America.Teotihuacan: The vast ancient city near Mexico City has the Pyramid of the Sun, and it stands in Mexico.
Landmarks in South America.Tikal: A Maya city in the jungles of Guatemala, in Central America, whose temples rise above the trees.
Landmarks in South America.Panama Canal: The canal links the Atlantic and Pacific in Central America, and was opened in 1914.
Landmarks in South America.Grand Canyon: The Arizona canyon is about 446 km long, and it lies in North America.
Landmarks in South America.Niagara Falls: On the Canada and US border, these falls move about 168,000 cubic meters of water a minute at their peak.
Landmarks in South America.Havana: The capital of Cuba is in the Caribbean, famous for its vintage American cars.
Landmarks in South America.Tulum: A Maya walled city on a cliff over the Caribbean in Mexico, not South America.
Landmarks in South America.Copán: Honduras holds this Maya site, known for its hieroglyphic stairway, so it is in Central America.
Landmarks in South America.Monteverde: A cloud forest reserve in Costa Rica, home to the resplendent quetzal.
Landmarks in South America.Arenal Volcano: A conical volcano in Costa Rica, which was active for decades until 2010.
Landmarks in South America.Antigua Guatemala: A colonial city in Guatemala, ringed by volcanoes and filled with ruined churches.

Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Iron: Its symbol Fe comes from Latin ferrum. Earth's core is mostly iron, and its flow is what generates the planet's magnetic field.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Lead: Pb comes from Latin plumbum, the root of the word plumber, because Romans made water pipes from it.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Gold: Au comes from Latin aurum, meaning shining dawn. Gold is so soft that a single gram can be hammered into a sheet about a square meter wide.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Silver: Ag comes from Latin argentum, which also named the country Argentina. It is the best electrical conductor of any metal.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Sodium: Na comes from natrium, tied to natron, a salt Egyptians used for mummification. Sodium explodes in water but is safe in table salt.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Potassium: K comes from kalium, from the Arabic al-qali for ashes, because it was first extracted from wood ash.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Tin: Sn comes from Latin stannum. Mixed with copper, it made bronze, giving a whole age of history its name.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Mercury: Hg comes from Greek-Latin hydrargyrum, meaning liquid silver. It is the only metal liquid at room temperature.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Antimony: Sb comes from Latin stibium. Ancient Egyptians ground antimony compounds into eye makeup called kohl.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Tungsten: W comes from wolfram, its German name. Its melting point is above 3,400 degrees Celsius, the highest of any metal.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Copper: A trap: its symbol Cu looks Latin but it's only a short form of cuprum. Cyprus, where Romans mined it, gave the name, yet the symbol uses the same first letters.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Zinc: A trap: its symbol Zn comes straight from its English name, even though many metals use Latin. Zinc plus copper makes brass.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Carbon: A trap: C is simply its English name's first letter. The word comes from Latin carbo, meaning coal or charcoal.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Helium: A trap: He follows its English name, from Greek helios, the Sun, where it was first detected in 1868.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Calcium: A trap: Ca matches its English name, from Latin calx for lime. Chalk, limestone and seashells are all calcium compounds.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Chlorine: A trap: Cl follows the English name, from Greek chloros meaning pale green, the color of the gas.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Neon: A trap: Ne matches the English name, from Greek neos meaning new. It was discovered in 1898 by Ramsay and Travers.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Nickel: A trap: Ni matches English. The name comes from German miners' slang, Kupfernickel, meaning devil's copper, since the ore fooled them.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Platinum: A trap: Pt matches English. Its name comes from Spanish platina, little silver; early conquistadors considered it a nuisance in gold mines.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Oxygen: A trap: O matches English. Its name means acid-former in Greek, because Lavoisier wrongly believed all acids contain it.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Magnesium: A trap: Mg matches English. It burns with a blinding white flame and was once used in camera flashes.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Uranium: A trap: U matches English. It is named after the planet Uranus, discovered just eight years before the element.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Aluminum: A trap: Al matches the name. Once rarer than gold, it was so precious that Napoleon III served his top guests with aluminum cutlery.
Elements whose symbol starts with anothe.Sulfur: A trap: S matches English. Also spelled sulphur, it was burned in ancient times as brimstone to fumigate buildings.

Things that conduct electricity.Copper: The standard wire metal, and second only to silver in conductivity; most wiring in your walls is copper.
Things that conduct electricity.Silver: The best conductor of all metals, but too costly for ordinary wires, so it's used in key electronics contacts.
Things that conduct electricity.Gold: Slightly less conductive than copper, yet it never corrodes, which is why connectors in phones and spacecraft are gold-plated.
Things that conduct electricity.Aluminum: Conducts about 60 percent as well as copper but is much lighter, so overhead power lines are mostly aluminum.
Things that conduct electricity.Iron: Conducts, though much worse than copper; it's more known for being magnetic than for carrying current.
Things that conduct electricity.Salt water: Dissolved salt splits into charged ions that carry current, which is why electrical devices are dangerous near the sea.
Things that conduct electricity.Graphite: A nonmetal that conducts, because carbon atoms in its layers have loose electrons, and it's used in battery electrodes.
Things that conduct electricity.Steel: An iron alloy that conducts moderately well; power-line cables often have steel cores for strength.
Things that conduct electricity.Mercury: The only metal liquid at room temperature, and it conducts, which made it handy for old tilt switches.
Things that conduct electricity.Human body: Mostly through salty fluids, which is why wet skin conducts much better than dry, and why electrical safety around water matters.
Things that conduct electricity.Brass: A copper-zinc alloy that conducts well, which is why many electrical plugs have brass pins.
Things that conduct electricity.Tin foil: Metal foil conducts, so putting it in a microwave can produce sparks, since current flows in the thin edges.
Things that conduct electricity.Lemon juice: The acid releases ions, so lemons can power a small clock if you stick copper and zinc into them.
Things that conduct electricity.Rubber: A trap: electrons can't move freely in it, so it insulates, which is why electricians' gloves are made of it.
Things that conduct electricity.Glass: A trap: it's an excellent insulator at room temperature, which is why power lines hang from glass or ceramic insulators.
Things that conduct electricity.Dry wood: A trap: dry wood insulates, but wet wood conducts, which is why trees get hit by lightning.
Things that conduct electricity.Plastic: A trap: it insulates, which is why wires are coated in it, though special polymers won a Nobel Prize for conducting.
Things that conduct electricity.Paper: A trap: dry paper is an insulator, and was used to wrap early electrical cables.
Things that conduct electricity.Wool: A trap: it traps charge when rubbed rather than conducting it, which is why sweaters give static shocks.
Things that conduct electricity.Porcelain: A trap: a ceramic insulator, used on utility poles and in old fuse boxes.
Things that conduct electricity.Diamond: A trap: pure diamond is an electrical insulator, yet it conducts heat better than any metal.
Things that conduct electricity.Styrofoam: A trap: foamed plastic insulates both electricity and heat, and it is mostly air.
Things that conduct electricity.Cotton: A trap: dry cotton insulates and was once wrapped around wires as an insulator.
Things that conduct electricity.Teflon: A trap: PTFE is a superb insulator, which is why it lines high-quality cables, and it is also non-stick.

Star Wars characters.Luke Skywalker: Luke's name was Luke Starkiller in early drafts. He grew up on Tatooine and became a Jedi.
Star Wars characters.Darth Vader: Vader's breathing was made by sound designer Ben Burtt recording scuba gear. James Earl Jones supplied the voice.
Star Wars characters.Yoda: Yoda was played by a puppet created by Stuart Freeborn and voiced by Frank Oz. In the film he's about 900 years old.
Star Wars characters.Chewbacca: Chewbacca is a Wookiee whose growls were made from animal recordings, including bears, lions and walruses.
Star Wars characters.Han Solo: Harrison Ford played Han Solo, and his line 'I know' to Leia was ad-libbed in The Empire Strikes Back.
Star Wars characters.Leia: Princess Leia's famous side buns were inspired by the hairstyles of women in the Mexican Revolution.
Star Wars characters.R2-D2: The name came from 'Reel 2, Dialog 2', an editing term George Lucas heard on set. Kenny Baker sat inside the droid in many scenes.
Star Wars characters.C-3PO: C-3PO is a droid fluent in over six million forms of communication, played by Anthony Daniels. He's the only actor in all the main films.
Star Wars characters.Obi-Wan Kenobi: Alec Guinness played him in 1977. He disliked the film's dialogue but his fee percentage made him wealthy.
Star Wars characters.Boba Fett: Boba Fett has little screen time in the original trilogy, but his mysterious armor made him a fan favorite.
Star Wars characters.Jabba the Hutt: Jabba was a large puppet operated by several people. He's a crime lord who keeps Han Solo frozen in carbonite.
Star Wars characters.Grogu: Grogu, called 'Baby Yoda', debuted in The Mandalorian in 2019. He's the same species as Yoda but his origins are unknown.
Star Wars characters.Spock: Spock is the half-Vulcan from Star Trek, played by Leonard Nimoy. Wrong franchise, as it's a famous mix-up.
Star Wars characters.Captain Kirk: William Shatner played Kirk in Star Trek. This is a different space saga from Star Wars.
Star Wars characters.Worf: Worf is a Klingon officer from Star Trek: The Next Generation. He's not in Star Wars, though he's got a space warrior look.
Star Wars characters.Picard: Jean-Luc Picard captains the Enterprise in Star Trek. The two sagas are rivals in fans' hearts, but not in the same universe.
Star Wars characters.Uhura: Nichelle Nichols' Uhura was a communications officer in Star Trek and an early Black woman in a leading TV role.
Star Wars characters.Neo: Neo is the hero of The Matrix, played by Keanu Reeves. Not Star Wars, though both have a chosen one.
Star Wars characters.Morpheus: Morpheus offers Neo the red pill or blue pill in The Matrix. He is named after the Greek god of dreams.
Star Wars characters.Ripley: Ripley is the heroine of the Alien films, played by Sigourney Weaver. Different space adventure.
E.T. is Spielberg's friendly alien from 1982, who wanted to 'phone home'. Not from Star Wars.
Star Wars characters.Optimus Prime: Optimus Prime is the Autobot leader of the Transformers franchise. He's not in Star Wars.
Star Wars characters.Marty McFly: Marty McFly travels in time in Back to the Future, in a DeLorean. He isn't in a galaxy far, far away.
Star Wars characters.Flash Gordon: Flash Gordon was a 1930s space-adventure hero, and Lucas wanted to remake the serials, then created Star Wars instead.

Alfred Hitchcock films.Psycho: The shower scene has about 78 camera setups for roughly 45 seconds. Hitchcock reportedly used chocolate syrup as blood in the black-and-white film.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Vertigo: The film introduced the dolly zoom, a camera trick that mimics the feeling of vertigo. It was a flop in 1958 but later topped critics' polls.
Alfred Hitchcock films.The Birds: The 1963 thriller has no musical score, using electronic bird sounds instead. Actress Tippi Hedren endured days of real birds thrown at her.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Rear Window: Almost the entire film is shot from one apartment, with a huge set built on a soundstage. James Stewart plays a photographer with a broken leg.
Alfred Hitchcock films.North by Northwest: It features the famous crop duster chase and a finale on Mount Rushmore. Cary Grant plays an ad executive mistaken for a spy.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Rebecca: Rebecca (1940) won the Best Picture Oscar, Hitchcock's only film to do so. Rebecca herself never appears on screen.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Rope: Rope (1948) is filmed to look like a few continuous takes, with hidden cuts. It's based on the real 1924 Leopold and Loeb case.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Notorious: This 1946 thriller with Ingrid Bergman and Cary Grant features uranium hidden in wine bottles, years before the atomic age was widely known.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Dial M for Murder: Hitchcock shot this 1954 thriller in 3D, though most audiences first saw it flat. Grace Kelly stars as a wife targeted by her husband.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Strangers on a Train: Based on Patricia Highsmith's first novel, it proposes two strangers swap murders. It was made in 1951.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Jaws: Spielberg's 1975 shark thriller shaped the summer blockbuster, but Hitchcock had no hand in it.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Halloween: John Carpenter made it in 1978 on a tiny budget. Its star Jamie Lee Curtis is the daughter of Janet Leigh, Psycho's shower victim.
Alfred Hitchcock films.The Shining: Stanley Kubrick made this 1980 horror film, famed for its long Steadicam shots. Hitchcock died that year.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Taxi Driver: Martin Scorsese directed this 1976 film with Robert De Niro, who improvised the line 'You talkin' to me?'.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Citizen Kane: Orson Welles made Citizen Kane in 1941, often named the greatest film ever. It's Welles, not Hitchcock.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Casablanca: Casablanca (1942) was directed by Michael Curtiz and won Best Picture. Hitchcock had no part in it.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Chinatown: Roman Polanski directed this 1974 neo-noir, and Robert Towne won an Oscar for the script.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Goodfellas: Scorsese's 1990 gangster film is a classic, with a famous long tracking shot through the Copacabana club.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Seven: David Fincher directed this 1995 thriller, ending on the shocking line 'What's in the box?'. Not Hitchcock.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Scream: Wes Craven made this slasher in 1996, which winks at horror movie rules. It also pays tribute to Psycho by killing its star early.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Alien: Ridley Scott directed Alien in 1979. Like Psycho, it famously shocks viewers by killing a main character.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Les Diaboliques: Henri-Georges Clouzot's 1955 French thriller, with a famous bathtub twist, is a close cousin of Psycho in spirit. Hitchcock didn't direct it.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Get Out: Jordan Peele's 2017 horror film won an Oscar for original screenplay. Not Hitchcock, though its tension owes him.
Alfred Hitchcock films.Carrie: Brian De Palma made Carrie in 1976, from Stephen King's first novel. He often borrowed from Hitchcock, but it's not his.

Batman's allies (not enemies).Ace the Bat-Hound: A German shepherd who debuted in 1955 as Batman's canine crime-fighting partner, complete with a mask.
Batman's allies (not enemies).Joker: Batman's arch-enemy since 1940, he was designed to resemble Conrad Veidt's grinning face from The Man Who Laughs.
Batman's allies (not enemies).Penguin: Oswald Cobblepot's look, according to Bob Kane, was inspired by a penguin mascot in a cigarette ad.
Batman's allies (not enemies).Riddler: Edward Nygma, whom Frank Gorshin played on the 1966 TV show in a role that earned an Emmy nomination.
Batman's allies (not enemies).Bane: He broke Batman's back in the 1993 Knightfall storyline, and he's a strategist as much as a brute.

Batman's allies (not enemies).Scarecrow: Dr. Jonathan Crane uses fear toxin; Cillian Murphy played him in Nolan's Batman Begins.
Batman's allies (not enemies).Mr. Freeze: He was originally Mr. Zero and was renamed Mr. Freeze after the 1960s TV show used the new name.
Batman's allies (not enemies).Poison Ivy: A trap: Pamela Isley is a villain, but she has often been written as an antihero and occasional ally.

Batman's allies (not enemies).Hush: Thomas Elliot, Bruce Wayne's childhood friend turned enemy, was introduced in the 2002 Hush storyline.
Batman's allies (not enemies).Mad Hatter: Jervis Tetch, a mind-control villain obsessed with Alice in Wonderland.
Batman's allies (not enemies).Clayface: The first, Basil Karlo, was an actor, and his name is a pun on horror star Boris Karloff.
Batman's allies (not enemies).Hugo Strange: A psychiatrist who deduced Batman's secret identity in 1940, among his earliest foes.
Batman's allies (not enemies).Black Mask: Roman Sionis, a crime boss in a skull-like mask, was played by Ewan McGregor in Birds of Prey.

Engines on Thomas & Friends.Postman Pat: Postman Pat is a British mail carrier with a black-and-white cat, Jess, who lives in Greendale.
Engines on Thomas & Friends.Fireman Sam: Fireman Sam is a Welsh firefighter from Pontypandy, in his own show, and not part of Thomas's railway.

Characters who are medical doctors.Sheldon Cooper: Sheldon has a PhD in physics, not medicine, which he often reminds people. He is a doctor of science, not a medical one.
Characters who are medical doctors.Indiana Jones: Dr. Henry Jones Jr. holds a doctorate in archaeology, not medicine. The name Indiana came from director George Lucas's own Alaskan malamute.
Characters who are medical doctors.Doc Brown: Emmett Brown is a scientist with a doctorate in physics, not medicine. His flux capacitor needs 1.21 gigawatts to time travel.

Instruments played with a keyboard.Piano: Its full name, pianoforte, means 'soft-loud', because Cristofori's early 1700s invention could play at different volumes, unlike the harpsichord.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Organ: The pipe organ, with thousands of pipes and several keyboards, is sometimes called the 'king of instruments', and the largest are the biggest instruments in the world.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Harpsichord: Its strings are plucked rather than hammered, so the player can't make notes louder by pressing harder, unlike a piano.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Synthesizer: Robert Moog's 1960s synthesizers brought the instrument to rock and pop, and made it a standard instrument by the 1970s.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Celesta: A keyboard that strikes metal plates with hammers, and Tchaikovsky's Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy made it famous.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Clavichord: A quiet early keyboard instrument whose strings are struck by metal tangents, which let players add vibrato, and Bach loved it.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Keytar: A keyboard worn like a guitar on a strap, popular in 1980s pop and used by Herbie Hancock.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Harmonium: A reed organ pumped by foot pedals, and it is essential to Indian devotional music and qawwali.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Electric piano: The Rhodes electric piano uses hammers hitting small metal tines, giving a bell-like sound heard in countless 1970s songs.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Xylophone: It is played with mallets, not keys, and so is a percussion instrument, though it has the same piano-like layout of bars.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Marimba: Struck with mallets, this keyboard-shaped percussion instrument has no keys to press, so it is not a true keyboard instrument.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Vibraphone: Players strike its metal bars with mallets, with a motor spinning discs that create its trademark vibrato, but it has no keyboard.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Glockenspiel: Mallets strike its metal bars, so it isn't a keyboard instrument. The celesta looks like a small piano and sounds similar, but it does have keys.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Harp: A plucked string instrument, with no keys; the player's fingers touch the strings directly.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Zither: A string instrument that is plucked or strummed with the fingers, with no keys, despite its flat, tabletop look.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Dulcimer: Its strings are struck by small hammers, like a piano's ancestor, but the player holds the hammers, not keys.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Steel drum: Made from oil barrels, the Trinidadian steel pan is struck with mallets, and the player uses no keys.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Kalimba: A thumb piano, whose tines are plucked directly with the thumbs, and it has no keys to press, despite the nickname.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Guitar: Its frets and strings are pressed and plucked directly by the hands, not played via a keyboard.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Cello: A bowed string instrument, so the player touches the strings directly, with no keyboard.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Trumpet: A brass instrument that has three valves, and its piston-style buttons don't make it a keyboard.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Flute: A woodwind with metal keys, but these are key mechanisms on the body, not a keyboard.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Banjo: A string instrument, played by plucking or strumming, so it has no keyboard, despite its drum-like body.
Instruments played with a keyboard.Bagpipes: A reed instrument blown through a bag, with finger holes on the chanter and no keyboard.

Operas (not musicals).Carmen: Bizet's 1875 premiere got a cool reception, but it's now among the most performed operas anywhere.
Operas (not musicals).Aida: Verdi's Egyptian drama, with a Triumphal March that sometimes features live animals on stage.
Operas (not musicals).Tosca: Puccini's thriller ends with the heroine leaping from Rome's Castel Sant'Angelo, and it premiered there in 1900.
Operas (not musicals).La Bohème: Puccini's tale of poor Parisian artists, whose story inspired the Broadway musical Rent.
Operas (not musicals).Madama Butterfly: Puccini's story set in Nagasaki, retold in the musical Miss Saigon, which moves it to Vietnam.
Operas (not musicals).The Magic Flute: Mozart's last big work, from 1791, includes the Queen of the Night's aria with its dazzling high F.
Operas (not musicals).Don Giovanni: Mozart's version of the Don Juan legend, which ends with the hero dragged down to hell.
Operas (not musicals).Rigoletto: Verdi's tragedy, adapted from a banned Victor Hugo play, with the famous La donna è mobile.
Operas (not musicals).Turandot: Puccini died before finishing it, and the aria Nessun dorma comes from this opera.
Operas (not musicals).La Traviata: Verdi's heartbreaking tale of a Parisian courtesan, from Dumas's The Lady of the Camellias.
Operas (not musicals).Fidelio: Beethoven's only opera, and he rewrote it several times before it succeeded.
Operas (not musicals).Cats: A musical based on T.S. Eliot's poems, whose Memory is its signature song, and not an opera.
Operas (not musicals).Les Misérables: A musical, though nearly all sung through like an opera, which makes it a classic trap.
Operas (not musicals).Phantom of the Opera: A musical set in an opera house, not an opera, though Lloyd Webber writes in a very operatic style.
Operas (not musicals).Rent: A rock musical, and a modern retelling of La Bohème, so not an opera despite the plot link.
Operas (not musicals).Miss Saigon: A musical retelling Madama Butterfly in Vietnam, so it's not an opera though its story is.
Operas (not musicals).Evita: A musical that is sung through, but Lloyd Webber and Rice created it as a rock opera-style musical, so it's a trap.
Operas (not musicals).Hamilton: A hip-hop musical and winner of the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, so not an opera.
Operas (not musicals).Wicked: A musical based on the Wizard of Oz backstory, among Broadway's biggest hits, so not an opera.
Operas (not musicals).Chicago: A jazz-age musical, and one of Broadway's longest-running shows, so not an opera.
Operas (not musicals).Oklahoma!: A 1943 Rodgers and Hammerstein musical often considered a turning point for the form, and not an opera.
Operas (not musicals).Grease: A rock-and-roll musical set in the 1950s, so not an opera, though it was later a hit film.
Operas (not musicals).Mamma Mia!: A musical built from ABBA songs, so it's a jukebox musical rather than an opera.
Operas (not musicals).Annie: A musical based on a comic strip, Little Orphan Annie, and so not an opera.

Bob Dylan songs.Blowin' in the Wind: Blowin' in the Wind (1963) became an anthem of the civil rights movement, and Peter, Paul and Mary had a hit with it.
Bob Dylan songs.Like a Rolling Stone: Like a Rolling Stone (1965) was unusually long for radio at over six minutes, and Rolling Stone once ranked it the greatest song ever.
Bob Dylan songs.Mr. Tambourine Man: Mr. Tambourine Man went to number one for The Byrds in 1965, who put the song to a folk-rock beat.
Bob Dylan songs.Tangled Up in Blue: Tangled Up in Blue is the opening of Blood on the Tracks (1975), with a story that shifts time and perspective.
Bob Dylan songs.Lay Lady Lay: Lay Lady Lay was written for the film Midnight Cowboy but arrived too late, and was released in 1969.
Bob Dylan songs.Just Like a Woman: Just Like a Woman is from Blonde on Blonde (1966), among the first double albums in rock.
Bob Dylan songs.It Ain't Me Babe: It Ain't Me Babe is from 1964's Another Side of Bob Dylan, and The Turtles had a hit with it.
Bob Dylan songs.Masters of War: Masters of War is a fierce anti-war song from 1963, aimed at arms makers, set to an old folk tune.
Bob Dylan songs.Desolation Row: Desolation Row runs over 11 minutes, closing Highway 61 Revisited with a cast of figures from history and fiction.
Bob Dylan songs.Imagine: Imagine is John Lennon's 1971 plea for peace, written after leaving the Beatles.
Bob Dylan songs.Respect: Respect was written by Otis Redding, and Aretha Franklin's 1967 version turned it into a feminist anthem.
Bob Dylan songs.Hallelujah: Hallelujah is Leonard Cohen's, from 1984, and it became famous through covers by John Cale and Jeff Buckley.
Bob Dylan songs.Suzanne: Suzanne is Leonard Cohen's, first heard in Judy Collins's 1966 recording, before he sang it himself.
Bob Dylan songs.Fast Car: Fast Car is Tracy Chapman's 1988 hit, and Luke Combs took it back up the charts decades later.
Bob Dylan songs.Big Yellow Taxi: Big Yellow Taxi is Joni Mitchell's, 1970, and its line about paving paradise was a landmark of environmental pop.
Bob Dylan songs.Both Sides Now: Both Sides Now is Joni Mitchell's, written when she was in her twenties, and she re-recorded it as an older woman.
Bob Dylan songs.The Sound of Silence: The Sound of Silence is Simon & Garfunkel's, and its 1966 version had electric guitar and drums added without the duo's input.
Bob Dylan songs.Mrs. Robinson: Mrs. Robinson is Simon & Garfunkel's, written for the film The Graduate.
Bob Dylan songs.American Pie: American Pie is Don McLean's 1971 epic, which runs over eight minutes and mourns the death of Buddy Holly.
Bob Dylan songs.Heart of Gold: Heart of Gold is Neil Young's only number-one single, from the 1972 album Harvest.
Bob Dylan songs.Born to Run: Born to Run is Bruce Springsteen's, from 1975, which made him a star.
Bob Dylan songs.Fire and Rain: Fire and Rain is James Taylor's, from 1970, with references to his friends and struggles.
Bob Dylan songs.Wonderwall: Wonderwall is Oasis's, from 1995, and one of the most-played songs by buskers.
Bob Dylan songs.Paint It Black: Paint It Black is the Rolling Stones' 1966 song, with sitar played by Brian Jones.

Oasis songs.Champagne Supernova: Paul Weller of The Jam plays guitar on this 1995 epic, whose title and meaning Noel Gallagher has admitted are nonsense.
Oasis songs.Live Forever: Noel wrote it as a reply to Nirvana's I Hate Myself and Want to Die; it became Oasis's first Top 10 UK hit.

Oasis songs.Some Might Say: Oasis's first UK number one, from 1995; the title is a playful, hesitant promise, sung with Liam's sneer.
Oasis songs.Whatever: Neil Innes of the Rutles got a writing credit after the tune resembled How Sweet to Be an Idiot.
Oasis songs.Little by Little: A 2002 single from Heathen Chemistry, a mellow Noel Gallagher song, and one of their later UK Top 10 hits.
Oasis songs.The Masterplan: This 1998 compilation title track began as the B-side of Wonderwall, and became a fan favorite instrumental.
Oasis songs.Rock 'n' Roll Star: The first track on Definitely Maybe, 1994, whose opening swirl of guitar feels like a statement of arrival.
Oasis songs.Slide Away: A Definitely Maybe closer, with Liam's tender vocal; Noel has called it one of his favorites.
Oasis songs.Song 2: Blur's 1997 anthem, famous for its Woo-hoo; many assume Oasis, but Blur was their rival.
Oasis songs.Parklife: Blur, 1994, narrated by actor Phil Daniels, whose cockney voice makes the Britpop snapshot.
Oasis songs.Girls & Boys: Blur's 1994 hit, made of synth-pop and a laddish guitar; Blur, not Oasis.
Oasis songs.Country House: Blur beat Oasis on the charts with it in 1995, the day of the Britpop chart war.
Oasis songs.Common People: Pulp, 1995. Jarvis Cocker wrote about a Greek art student wanting to live like normal people.

Oasis songs.Lucky Man: The Verve, 1997, from the Urban Hymns era; it's a good guess because the Verve was Oasis's friend, but not Oasis.
Oasis songs.Creep: Radiohead, 1992, a grunge-influenced hit; not Oasis.
Oasis songs.Yellow: Coldplay, 2000. Chris Martin's band was influenced by Britpop but isn't Oasis.
Oasis songs.Mr. Brightside: The Killers, 2003. An American band's hit, not from Manchester.
Oasis songs.Chasing Cars: Snow Patrol, 2006, a hit on Grey's Anatomy; not Oasis.
Oasis songs.Beautiful Day: U2's 2000 hit, from an Irish band that was bigger than Oasis in the 1990s; not Oasis.
Oasis songs.Sonnet: The Verve, 1997. Richard Ashcroft sang it; a Wigan band, and a close pal of Oasis, but another band.
