French singers.Charles Aznavour: He wrote over 1,000 songs and sold more than 100 million records, and he was French-Armenian.
French singers.Serge Gainsbourg: His 1969 duet "Je t'aime... moi non plus" with Jane Birkin was banned in several countries for being too steamy.
French singers.Johnny Hallyday: France's biggest rock star sold over 100 million records, and more than a million turned out for his 2017 funeral.
French singers.Françoise Hardy: A 1960s yé-yé icon who wrote "Tous les garçons et les filles", she also drew admiration from Bob Dylan.
French singers.Indila: The singer's 2014 hit "Dernière danse" drew hundreds of millions of YouTube views, and she mixes French with Eastern flavours.
French singers.Zaz: Isabelle Geffroy won attention busking in Paris, and her 2010 song "Je veux" blends jazz-manouche with chanson.
French singers.Vanessa Paradis: She broke out at 14 with "Joe le taxi", and she was long the face of Chanel.
French singers.Charles Trenet: His 1946 song "La Mer" was later covered as "Beyond the Sea", and he's known as "the Singing Fool".
French singers.Mireille Mathieu: She was discovered on a TV talent show in 1965 and is known for her helmet-like black hair and Edith Piaf comparisons.
French singers.Jacques Brel: He is Belgian, not French, though he lived in Paris; his song "Ne me quitte pas" became "If You Go Away" in English.
French singers.Céline Dion: She is Canadian, from a Quebec family of 14 children, though she sings in French too and became a global star.
French singers.Stromae: Paul Van Haver is Belgian, born in Brussels to a Rwandan father, and his hit "Alors on danse" went to No. 1 across Europe.
French singers.Petula Clark: A British singer who had a hit with "Downtown" in 1964, and she also recorded many songs in French.
French singers.Nana Mouskouri: The Greek singer, in her signature glasses, has recorded in many languages, including French, and has sold hundreds of millions of records.
French singers.Julio Iglesias: The Spaniard is among the best-selling Latin artists ever, and he had been a goalkeeper at Real Madrid's youth team.
French singers.Andrea Bocelli: Blind since age 12, the Italian tenor sold millions of albums, and he sang "Con te partirò".
French singers.Shakira: The Colombian singer's 2010 World Cup song "Waka Waka" was a global hit, and she writes in Spanish and English.
French singers.Björk: The Icelandic singer began recording as a child in 1977 and is famed for her wildly experimental sounds.
French singers.Enya: The Irish singer's layered, multitracked vocals made "Orinoco Flow" a hit, and she sings in Irish and English.
French singers.Kylie Minogue: The Australian pop star began on the soap "Neighbours" and had hits like "Can't Get You Out of My Head".
French singers.Laura Pausini: The Italian singer won Sanremo at 18 with 'La solitudine' and has sold millions of records, but she is Italian, not French.
French singers.Demis Roussos: The Greek singer of the 1970s was famed for his flowing kaftans and operatic voice, and he was born in Alexandria, Egypt.
French singers.Falco: The Austrian singer's 1985 "Rock Me Amadeus" topped the US charts, a rare feat for a German-language song.

Poker hands.Royal flush: Ace-high straight flush of one suit: 10-J-Q-K-A. The odds of being dealt one in five cards are about 1 in 650,000.
Poker hands.Straight flush: A straight flush that isn't royal still beats everything but one hand, roughly a 1-in-72,000 deal in five-card poker.
Poker hands.Four of a kind: Four matching ranks, such as four sevens. Players often call it quads; only the straight flush and royal flush rank higher.
Poker hands.Full house: Three of one rank plus a pair. Ties between full houses are decided by the three-of-a-kind rank first, not the pair.
Poker hands.Flush: Five cards of one suit, any order. It beats a straight, which surprises beginners since a straight feels harder to get.
Poker hands.Straight: Five consecutive ranks. The ace can play high or low, so A-2-3-4-5 (the wheel) is the lowest straight.
Poker hands.Three of a kind: Also called trips or a set, depending on whether you hold a pocket pair. It beats two pair but loses to any straight.
Poker hands.Two pair: Two different pairs plus a kicker. If both players hold the same top pair, the second pair and then the kicker break ties.
Poker hands.One pair: Just two matching ranks and three unrelated cards. It is the most common made hand, dealt roughly 42% of the time in five-card poker.
Poker hands.High card: When nothing else lines up, your best single card plays. It is the most common five-card hand, dealt about half the time.
Poker hands.Yahtzee: Yahtzee is a dice game, not cards. Its scoring borrows poker's words, such as full house and straight, and it was trademarked in 1956 after a yacht-board game.
Poker hands.Gin: Gin rummy is a two-player game of melding sets and runs, then knocking when your leftover cards are low. It has no poker-style ranking.
Poker hands.Rummy: Rummy is built on melding sets and runs, not ranking hands. It is the ancestor of gin, canasta and many draw-and-discard games.
Poker hands.Snap: Snap is a children's reaction game: slap the pile when two matching cards appear. No hand rankings are involved.
Poker hands.Blackjack: Blackjack is a card game of its own, scoring 21, not a ranked poker hand. Its name once referred to a bonus for an ace with a black jack.
Poker hands.Checkmate: Checkmate is chess. A chess board has no cards at all, and the word comes from the Persian shah mat, meaning the king is helpless.
Poker hands.Small straight: A Yahtzee category, not a poker hand: four consecutive dice score 30. In poker, four straight cards alone make nothing.
Poker hands.Large straight: The Yahtzee large straight (five in a row) scores 40. In poker, a straight is a ranked hand, but the dice version is a different game.
Poker hands.Bingo: Bingo is a numbers game of chance with called balls and cards. It has no ranking of hands, though its name suggests a win call.
Poker hands.Trump: A trump is a suit that outranks others in games like bridge or hearts. Poker has no trump; all suits are equal.
Poker hands.Grand slam: In bridge, a grand slam means winning all 13 tricks. It has nothing to do with poker hand rankings.
Poker hands.Bust: In blackjack, bust means going over 21 and losing at once. Poker players just fold; 'bust' only means losing all chips.
Poker hands.Natural: In blackjack, a natural is an ace plus a ten-value card, usually paid 3 to 2. Poker's best hand is the royal flush instead.
Poker hands.Crib: In cribbage, the crib is the extra hand formed from discards that the dealer scores. Poker has no equivalent.

Crafts done with a needle.Knitting: Two needles loop yarn into fabric. Knitted socks have been found in Egyptian tombs from around the 11th century.
Crafts done with a needle.Embroidery: Decorating cloth with thread stitches is ancient, and the Bayeux Tapestry is actually an embroidery, not a woven tapestry.
Crafts done with a needle.Cross-stitch: Small X-shaped stitches on a grid build up images, and they became popular samplers that girls used to practice their skills.
Crafts done with a needle.Quilting: Stitching layers of fabric and padding together makes warm bedding, and quilts have been made for centuries on several continents.
Crafts done with a needle.Sewing: A needle and thread is among the oldest technologies, and bone needles over 40,000 years old have been found in Siberia.
Crafts done with a needle.Needlepoint: Stitching through stiff open-weave canvas makes sturdy designs that cover cushions and chair seats. Wool is the classic yarn.
Crafts done with a needle.Darning: Weaving new threads across a hole mends worn socks, and a wooden mushroom used to hold the sock taut while stitching.
Crafts done with a needle.Needle felting: A barbed needle jabbed repeatedly tangles wool fibers into solid shapes, so it's used for sculpting small animals.
Crafts done with a needle.Patchwork: Sewing small fabric pieces into larger designs began as a thrifty way to reuse scraps, and later became an art form.
Crafts done with a needle.Crochet: It uses a hook, not a needle, to pull loops through each other. It looks like knitting but the tool tells the difference.
Crafts done with a needle.Origami: Japanese paper folding uses no needle, scissors or glue in the classical form. A traditional goal is a crane from one square sheet.
Crafts done with a needle.Pottery: Clay shaping and firing involves hands, wheels and kilns, not needles, though potters do use needle tools to trim.
Crafts done with a needle.Woodturning: A lathe spins wood against a chisel, so it's shaped by cutting tools rather than any needle.
Crafts done with a needle.Calligraphy: Beautiful writing uses pens or brushes, and the word comes from Greek for beautiful writing.
Crafts done with a needle.Macrame: The craft of knotting cords into patterns uses fingers alone, and sailors made it into decorative rope work.
Crafts done with a needle.Scrapbooking: Arranging photos and mementos on pages uses glue and scissors rather than needle and thread.
Crafts done with a needle.Decoupage: Pasting cut paper onto objects and varnishing it over is done with glue, and the name comes from the French for cutting out.
Crafts done with a needle.Whittling: Carving wood by hand with a small knife takes a blade, not a needle, and is a classic campfire pastime.
Crafts done with a needle.Candle making: Pouring wax around a wick makes candles with no needle involved, though some hobbyists use one to center wicks.
Crafts done with a needle.Soap making: Soap results from a chemical reaction between fats and lye, so it's chemistry, not needlework.
Crafts done with a needle.Juggling: Keeping objects in the air is a skill, not a craft, and it needs hands and practice rather than needles.
Crafts done with a needle.Birdwatching: Observing wild birds takes binoculars and patience, not needles, and is a hobby, not a craft.
Crafts done with a needle.Kite flying: Kites were invented in China over 2,000 years ago, and flying one takes wind and string, not needles.
Crafts done with a needle.Stamp collecting: Philately is a hobby of collecting rather than making, and it's among the world's most popular, but no needle is involved.

American football positions.Quarterback: The offence's passer and play-caller; a top NFL quarterback must read the defence in seconds, and the helmet has a radio for the coach.
American football positions.Running back: Carries handoffs and also catches passes; the NFL single-season rushing record is over 2,100 yards, set by Eric Dickerson in 1984.
American football positions.Wide receiver: Lines up wide to catch passes; the best get open with precise routes and then must hold on to the ball under heavy contact.
American football positions.Tight end: Part blocker, part receiver, and the one offensive position lining up on either end of the line, next to the tackle.
American football positions.Linebacker: Plays behind the defensive line, stopping runs and covering passes, and often wears the helmet radio for the defence.
American football positions.Cornerback: Covers wide receivers one on one; the position needs the speed to match the fastest players on the field.
American football positions.Safety: The last line of defence, deep in the secondary; the name is also what a two-point score for tackling in the end zone is called.
American football positions.Kicker: Handles field goals and extra points; a field goal of over 60 yards is rare enough to make highlight reels.
American football positions.Punter: Kicks the ball away on fourth down, trying to pin the opponent deep; the best can boom it 50 or more yards.
American football positions.Nose tackle: A heavy defensive lineman who lines up opposite the centre, often 330 pounds or more, taking on double teams.
American football positions.Defensive end: Rushes the quarterback from the edge, and the NFL career sack record of 200 belongs to Bruce Smith.
American football positions.Long snapper: A specialist who snaps the ball back on punts and field goals, a job few people notice until a snap goes wrong.
American football positions.Shortstop: A baseball infielder; football has no bases, so no one is stationed between second and third.
American football positions.Pitcher: A baseball player who throws from a mound, not an American football position.
American football positions.Catcher: A baseball position behind home plate; football's catchers are receivers.
American football positions.Point guard: A basketball position, the team's ball handler and playmaker, not an American football role.
American football positions.Goalkeeper: Soccer's last line of defence; American football has no goal to guard.
American football positions.Striker: A soccer forward, not an American football position.
American football positions.Winger: A soccer position along the flank; football has wide receivers instead.
American football positions.Wicketkeeper: A cricket role behind the stumps, so cricket, not football.
American football positions.Fly-half: A rugby union playmaker, roughly the quarterback of rugby, but not an American football role.
American football positions.Scrum-half: A rugby union position that feeds the scrum, so not part of American football.
American football positions.Setter: A volleyball playmaker, so not part of football.
American football positions.Sweeper: A soccer defender who sweeps up behind the back line, not an American football position.

Sports gear that has strings.Tennis racket: Modern strings are often synthetic gut, but natural gut from cow intestines is still used by top professionals; Roger Federer used a hybrid.
Sports gear that has strings.Badminton racket: Strung at higher tension than tennis rackets, and the lightest frames weigh under 100 grams, so a smash can send the shuttle past 400 km/h.
Sports gear that has strings.Squash racket: The strings are thinner than a tennis racket's, and the frame is lighter, at about 120 to 140 grams.
Sports gear that has strings.Racquetball racket: Short-handled and sold with a wrist cord, as the fast rubber ball can easily fly out of a loose grip.
Sports gear that has strings.Lacrosse stick: Its pocket is made of mesh or string, a design descended from Indigenous stickball sticks that used netted rawhide.
Sports gear that has strings.Bow: Its string stores the energy of the bent limbs and releases it in a split second, sending an arrow at over 200 mph from a modern compound bow.
Sports gear that has strings.Crossbow: A horizontal bow whose string is cranked back and held, and medieval versions could pierce armour; it was once banned by a papal decree.
Sports gear that has strings.Kite: Flown on a line that can be hundreds of metres long; sports kites use lines strong enough to drag a buggy or lift a kitesurfer off the water.
Sports gear that has strings.Yo-yo: Its string is looped around the axle, so the toy can spin freely in place, which is the basis for tricks such as sleeping.
Sports gear that has strings.Hockey stick: A trap: the ice hockey stick's blade is solid wood or composite, with no netting or strings, unlike a lacrosse stick's pocket.
Sports gear that has strings.Baseball bat: A solid wood or aluminium shaft, which makes it a one-piece tool with no strings attached.
Sports gear that has strings.Golf club: A solid metal or composite shaft and head, so nothing is strung.
Sports gear that has strings.Table tennis paddle: A wood blade covered in rubber, with no strings, which is why it is called a paddle, not a racket in some places.
Sports gear that has strings.Pickleball paddle: A solid-faced paddle, not a stringed racket, which sets it apart from tennis and badminton.
Sports gear that has strings.Cricket bat: A single piece of willow, with a cane handle, so it does not use strings at all.
Sports gear that has strings.Javelin: A solid spear; its only winding is a cord grip around the middle, not strings for the playing surface.
Sports gear that has strings.Discus: A solid disc with a metal rim, and no strings.
Sports gear that has strings.Shuttlecock: A feathered cork cone used in badminton; it is hit by a stringed racket, but has none itself, and the best ones use goose feathers.
Sports gear that has strings.Frisbee: A moulded plastic disc, with no strings, whose flight relies on spin and its curved shape.
Sports gear that has strings.Skateboard: A wooden deck with wheels, with no strings involved.
Sports gear that has strings.Surfboard: Tied to the surfer's ankle by a leash, but that cord only stops it drifting; the board itself is solid foam or fibreglass, not strung.
Sports gear that has strings.Pool cue: A tapered wooden or composite stick, with a leather tip, and nothing strung.
Sports gear that has strings.Oar: A solid shaft with a blade, with no strings.
Sports gear that has strings.Hurley: The wooden stick of Irish hurling has a flat blade called a bas, with no strings, and the ball, a sliotar, is hit with it.

At a medieval European feast.Roast boar: A wild pig, a medieval delicacy. Hunting it was a noble sport, and a boar's head carried in was the centerpiece of feasts like Christmas.
At a medieval European feast.Mead: A honey wine, one of the oldest alcoholic drinks. Mead was so central to Old English halls that Beowulf's is a 'mead-hall'.
At a medieval European feast.Minstrel: A travelling musician-poet who sang at courts and feasts, and spread news and songs across Europe.
At a medieval European feast.Jester: A court entertainer in motley, who was sometimes allowed to say what no one else dared to the lord.
At a medieval European feast.Trencher: A slice of stale bread used as a plate. After the meal, the soaked trencher could be eaten or given to the poor.
At a medieval European feast.Roast peacock: The bird was roasted, skinned, and sometimes sewn back into its feathers for show, and it was served for the wealthy.
At a medieval European feast.Goblet: A drinking cup, often shared at high tables. Rich ones were silver or gold, while commoners used wooden or pottery cups.
At a medieval European feast.Venison: Deer meat, a noble's meal. Peasants who hunted deer risked severe punishment in forests belonging to the king.
At a medieval European feast.Spiced wine: Wine heated with cinnamon, ginger and cloves, called hippocras. Medieval cooks used spices to show wealth.
At a medieval European feast.Ale: The everyday drink of medieval Europe, safer than water, was brewed without hops until the late Middle Ages.
At a medieval European feast.Candles: A costly luxury; beeswax candles were for churches and nobles, while commoners used tallow ones that smelled and smoked.
At a medieval European feast.Meat pie: Called pasties or pies, with the crust often a thick 'coffin' not eaten, simply a baking dish.
At a medieval European feast.Roast turkey: Trap: turkeys come from the Americas and reached Europe only after 1492, so medieval feasts had no turkey.
At a medieval European feast.Potatoes: Trap: potatoes came from the Andes and arrived in Europe in the 1500s, after the Middle Ages.
At a medieval European feast.Tomato sauce: Trap: tomatoes were also from the Americas, and Europeans didn't eat them until the 1500s or later.
At a medieval European feast.Chocolate cake: Trap: chocolate was a Mesoamerican drink that reached Europe in the 1500s, and cake as we know it came later.
At a medieval European feast.Coffee: Trap: coffee reached Europe only in the 1600s, centuries after medieval feasts, so no cups were poured.
At a medieval European feast.French fries: Trap: fries need potatoes, which reached Europe only in the 1500s, after the Middle Ages.
At a medieval European feast.Pineapple: Trap: pineapples are from South America, and in Europe in the 1600s they were so rare that they were rented for display.
At a medieval European feast.Hot chocolate: Trap: drinking chocolate came from Aztec culture and reached Spain only in the 1500s.
At a medieval European feast.Chili con carne: Trap: chili peppers and beans come from the Americas, so it is a New World dish, not a medieval one.
At a medieval European feast.Popcorn: Trap: popcorn comes from maize, a New World crop, so it was unknown in medieval Europe.
At a medieval European feast.Tea: Trap: tea arrived in Europe in the 1600s, so no medieval feast served it, only ale and wine.
At a medieval European feast.Corn on the cob: Trap: maize is a New World crop, unknown in Europe until after Columbus in 1492, so no corn on the cob.

Things used for doing laundry.Washing machine: Front-loaders use far less water than old top-loaders, and the spin cycle can fling clothes around at over 1,000 rotations a minute.
Things used for doing laundry.Tumble dryer: Lint from a dryer is a real fire hazard, which is why the filter should be emptied after every load.
Things used for doing laundry.Laundry basket: Plastic baskets with cut-out sides are not just for airflow; the holes also make them easy to grip on the hip.
Things used for doing laundry.Detergent: Modern detergents contain enzymes that digest protein and fat stains, which is why they work well even in cool water.
Things used for doing laundry.Fabric softener: It works by coating fibers with a slick, waxy film, which makes towels softer but also less absorbent over time.
Things used for doing laundry.Clothespins: The classic one-piece wooden clothespin was patented in America in the 1850s, and the basic spring design came later.
Things used for doing laundry.Drying rack: Air-drying indoors can add a surprising amount of moisture to a room, since a single load can release a liter or more of water.
Things used for doing laundry.Clothesline: Sunlight is a mild natural disinfectant and bleach, so line-dried whites often come out brighter than machine-dried ones.
Things used for doing laundry.Dryer sheets: They deposit a thin slippery coating on fabric that reduces static cling, which is why they can also reduce towel absorbency.
Things used for doing laundry.Stain remover: Most work on the principle that different stains need different chemistry: enzymes for proteins like blood, oxidizers for tea and wine.
Things used for doing laundry.Laundry pods: Their film is a water-soluble plastic called PVA that dissolves in the wash, but its bright, candy-like look has made storage safety a big concern.
Things used for doing laundry.Dishwasher: It washes dishes, not clothes. A dishwasher also uses less water than hand washing the same load, often just a few gallons.
Things used for doing laundry.Dish soap: It is made to cut grease on dishes and foams heavily, which would overflow a washing machine in a flood of suds.
Things used for doing laundry.Oven: Nothing laundry-related happens here. Self-cleaning ovens heat to around 900 degrees Fahrenheit to burn spills to ash.
Things used for doing laundry.Toaster: No laundry role. Early electric toasters in the 1900s had no auto pop-up, so burned toast was a daily hazard.
Things used for doing laundry.Blender: It belongs to the kitchen. Fred Osius patented the first blender in 1922, and it was built for mixing milkshakes.
Things used for doing laundry.Colander: It strains pasta, not clothes. Its name comes from the Latin word colare, meaning to strain.
Things used for doing laundry.Rolling pin: A baking tool for dough, not for laundry, though it flattens things the way mangles once pressed linens.
Things used for doing laundry.Whisk: A kitchen tool for whipping air into eggs and cream. Whipping egg whites in a copper bowl makes them more stable.
Things used for doing laundry.Frying pan: For cooking, not laundry. Cast iron pans can last for generations if seasoned and cared for properly.
Things used for doing laundry.Spatula: A flipping tool for the kitchen. In British English a spatula can also mean a flat medical instrument or a scraper.
Things used for doing laundry.Kettle: It boils water for tea, though it is water related. A kettle is not part of laundry, and the electric kettle dates to the 1890s.
Things used for doing laundry.Salad spinner: It spins water off lettuce, much like a washing machine spin cycle, but it is a kitchen tool, not a laundry one.
Things used for doing laundry.Dish rack: It dries dishes, not clothes, even though it looks a lot like a drying rack. The shape fits plates upright to drain.

Things that roll.Ball: Balls are among the oldest toys; rubber balls were made by Mesoamericans thousands of years ago.
Things that roll.Wheel: The wheel seems ancient yet it was invented only around 3500 BC, long after boats and pottery.
Things that roll.Marble: Marbles have been found in ancient Egypt and Rome, and the modern glass marble is machine-made from molten glass.
Things that roll.Log: Logs were used as rollers to move heavy stones, and some think pyramids were built this way.
Things that roll.Dice: Dice are a trap: they're cubes with flat faces, but they tumble and roll, and their roll is meant to be random.
Things that roll.Tumbleweed: Tumbleweeds are plants that dry out and break off, scattering their seeds as the wind blows them across plains.
Things that roll.Orange: An orange is a sphere-like fruit that rolls, and 'orange' the color was named after the fruit, not the other way around.
Things that roll.Bowling ball: Bowling balls can weigh up to 16 pounds, and their finger holes are drilled to fit your hand.
Things that roll.Barrel: Barrels roll on their curved sides, and old brewers and shippers rolled them across docks rather than carrying their heavy loads.
Things that roll.Tire: Early tires were solid rubber; John Dunlop's 1888 air-filled version, made for his son's bicycle, changed everything.
Things that roll.Hamster ball: A hamster ball lets a hamster roam the room safely, but vets say to keep sessions short and away from stairs.
Things that roll.Snowball: Snowballs grow as they roll, picking up snow; the same effect gave rise to the phrase 'snowball effect'.
Things that roll.Rolling pin: A rolling pin presses dough flat; some French ones are tapered and have no handles, giving more control.
Things that roll.Brick: A trap: a brick has flat sides and corners, so it slides or tumbles rather than rolls.
Things that roll.Book: A book is flat and rectangular, so it flops and slides rather than rolling, unless it's a scroll, which is built to roll.
Things that roll.Shoe: A shoe is lumpy and uneven, so it flops when thrown rather than rolling smoothly.
Things that roll.Table: A table has legs and a flat top, so it won't roll unless casters are added, as on restaurant carts.
Things that roll.Cardboard box: A cardboard box has corners and flat sides, so it tumbles or slides rather than rolling.
Things that roll.Ruler: A ruler is flat and thin, so it slides; only a round pencil-shaped one would roll off a desk.
Things that roll.Couch: A couch is a heavy rectangular lump, and without wheels it's nearly impossible to roll anywhere.
Things that roll.Fork: A fork is flat with prongs, so it slides or spins around instead of rolling.
Things that roll.Pyramid: A pyramid is a shape of flat triangular faces on a square base, so it can only tip, not roll.
Things that roll.Laptop: A laptop is a flat, hinged box, so it can't roll; its screen opens to about 180 degrees, though.
Things that roll.Stapler: A stapler has a flat base and a hinged arm, so it can slide across a desk but never rolls.

Things a mail carrier delivers.Letters: Still a core of the mail. In the US, the Postal Service handles over 100 billion pieces of mail a year.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Parcels: With online shopping, parcels now make up a growing share of what carriers bring to doors.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Postcards: Picture postcards gained popularity in the late 1800s. Some old postcards sell to collectors for a lot of money.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Bills: Utility and credit card bills have long been mailed. Many people now get them by email instead.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Magazines: Subscription magazines arrive in the mail, and the Postal Service's cheap periodical rates helped build the US magazine industry.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Catalogs: Sears catalogs once brought goods to rural homes. They even sold entire house kits by mail.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Junk mail: Unsolicited advertising makes up a big portion of what people receive. Americans get tens of billions of pieces yearly.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Greeting cards: Holiday seasons are the busiest times for mail. The first commercial Christmas card was sent in London in 1843.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Packages: Carriers bring everything from books to medicine. They deliver millions daily during peak season.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Flyers: Local advertising leaflets often arrive in mailboxes. Some are delivered as 'saturation mail' to every address on a route.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Pizza: A delivery driver brings pizza. The mail carrier works for the postal service, not restaurants.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Emails: Sent over the internet and instant. No mail carrier is involved.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Text messages: Travel over phone networks. The first SMS, in 1992, said 'Merry Christmas'.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Phone calls: Travel by wire or wireless, with no mail carrier in the loop.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Taxi rides: Drivers carry people, not mail. Taxis predate cars, back to horse-drawn hackneys.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Electricity: Supplied by utilities over power lines. Mail carriers don't deliver it.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Tweets: Posted online, now on X. They travel by internet, not by post.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Haircuts: A service, not a deliverable. Barbers have been trimming hair for centuries.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Sermons: Delivered from a pulpit. A mail carrier would only deliver a printed copy, not the sermon itself.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Sunshine: Delivered for free by the sun, which sends light across about 93 million miles in around eight minutes.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Tap water: Arrives through pipes. Mail carriers don't handle liquids like it.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Radio waves: Travel at the speed of light, which is infinitely faster than any carrier, and by air rather than by post.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Podcasts: Streamed or downloaded online. No mail carrier is involved.
Things a mail carrier delivers.Gossip: Spreads by word of mouth, not by mail. Carriers keep the contents of mail private by law.

Things in a hospital operating room.Operating table: Modern tables tilt, rotate and extend by remote control, so surgeons can reach a patient from any angle without moving them.
Things in a hospital operating room.Scalpel: Many surgical scalpels now use disposable blades that are sharper than a razor, and some are made of obsidian for ultra-fine incisions.
Things in a hospital operating room.Forceps: Obstetric forceps were kept as a family secret by the Chamberlen family of surgeons for roughly a century before becoming widely known.
Things in a hospital operating room.Retractor: Surgeons use these to hold tissue aside; some are self-retaining clamps, while others are held by an assistant for hours.
Things in a hospital operating room.Surgical lights: They are built to cast almost no shadow, using many small lamps so a surgeon's head or hands can't block the light.
Things in a hospital operating room.Anesthesia machine: It mixes oxygen with anesthetic gas and breathes for the patient, while sensors track the dose and blood oxygen every second.
Things in a hospital operating room.Heart monitor: The steady beep is deliberate: its pitch can change with blood oxygen level, so the team hears trouble without looking up.
Things in a hospital operating room.Sutures: Some are made to dissolve inside the body; ancient surgeons used flax, hair, and even the heads of biting ants to close wounds.
Things in a hospital operating room.Clamps: Hemostats clamp blood vessels shut to stop bleeding, and a surgeon may use dozens of them in a single long operation.
Things in a hospital operating room.Sterile drapes: These cover everything except the incision site, creating a sterile field where even a stray cough could be a risk.
Things in a hospital operating room.Suction tube: It clears blood and fluid so the surgeon can see; the fluid is measured to estimate how much blood the patient has lost.
Things in a hospital operating room.Gavel: Judges use it to demand order, but contrary to TV legend, many courts, especially in the UK, never use one at all.
Things in a hospital operating room.Easel: An easel holds a canvas upright; no surgeon would use one, but the word comes from the Dutch for donkey, since it carries the load.
Things in a hospital operating room.Jury box: Twelve jurors is a long tradition, though some courts use six, and the number comes from English common law.
Things in a hospital operating room.Pulpit: Preachers once climbed high pulpits so the voice carried; some medieval ones had sounding boards above them to project speech.
Things in a hospital operating room.Hay bale: Operating rooms are kept ultra clean, while hay sheds loose dust and spores that would be dangerous near an open wound.
Things in a hospital operating room.Jukebox: Surprisingly, music does play in many operating rooms, though it comes from a playlist or radio, not a coin-fed jukebox.
Things in a hospital operating room.Slot machine: Casino slots are built to deliver near misses on purpose, one reason they are rarely mistaken for medical equipment.
Things in a hospital operating room.Barber pole: A near-fit: barbers once also pulled teeth and let blood, and the red and white pole stands for blood and bandages.
Things in a hospital operating room.Trampoline: Absolutely not in the theater, though it does keep orthopedic surgeons in business with a steady supply of sprained ankles.
Things in a hospital operating room.Fire pole: Firefighters slide down them to save seconds; hospitals use stairs and lifts, and an operating room has no use for one.
Things in a hospital operating room.Car lift: A garage lifts cars hydraulically, and operating tables use similar hydraulic ideas, but this one is for the mechanic.
Things in a hospital operating room.Pizza oven: Instruments are sterilized in a steam autoclave at about 121 degrees Celsius, far gentler than a pizza oven at roughly 400.
Things in a hospital operating room.Hot tub: Warm water is great for relaxing, but a sterile operating room avoids standing warm water because bacteria love it.

Jobs ending in '-maker'.Watchmaker: Swiss watchmakers assemble movements with hundreds of parts smaller than a grain of rice, using tiny tools and magnifiers.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Dressmaker: Before ready-to-wear clothing in the 1900s, most women's dresses were made by a local dressmaker or at home.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Shoemaker: The fairy tale "The Elves and the Shoemaker" reflects how prized skilled shoemaking was, and the craft is called cordwaining.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Cabinetmaker: The term goes back to the 1600s, and a fine cabinetmaker uses dovetail joints, which hold without any nails.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Filmmaker: The Lumiere brothers held the first paid public film screening in Paris in 1895.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Toymaker: Toy making is old; dolls and toy animals have been found in ancient tombs, including Egyptian ones.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Clockmaker: Mechanical clocks appeared in Europe in the 1200s, long before they had faces, and the first rang bells to mark prayer hours.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Hatmaker: The word "mad as a hatter" is often linked to mercury used in hat felt, which damaged hatters' nerves.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Matchmaker: A traditional matchmaker arranges marriages, and a famous example is the matchmaker in "Fiddler on the Roof".
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Lawmaker: A lawmaker writes laws; in most countries these are elected representatives.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Bookmaker: A bookmaker takes bets rather than making books, and the name comes from recording bets in a book.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Haymaker: A haymaker is also a wild boxing punch, and not an occupation, though the phrase comes from swinging a scythe at hay.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Troublemaker: It describes behavior, not a paid trade, and no one has a business card with this written on it.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Pacemaker: A pacemaker is a device, not a person; the first was implanted in a human in 1958 in Sweden.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Peacemaker: It is a role or a nickname rather than a profession, and the Colt revolver of the Wild West got this nickname.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Noisemaker: A noisemaker is a party horn or rattle, an object rather than a job.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Merrymaker: It is someone who celebrates and has fun, a description and not a profession.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Mischief-maker: A person who causes mischief is a description, not an occupation.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Icemaker: A refrigerator machine, not a person, that freezes water into cubes.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Coffee maker: It is a machine, not an occupation, and the first drip coffee filter was invented by Melitta Bentz in 1908.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Holidaymaker: A British term for someone on vacation, so it is a status, not a profession.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Waffle maker: A kitchen appliance, and its name is a thing instead of a person, and Dutch settlers brought waffles to America.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Popcorn maker: It is a machine, not an occupation, and popcorn pops when water inside the kernel turns to steam.
Jobs ending in '-maker'.Yogurt maker: A device, not a job, and yogurt can be made at home with live bacteria and warm milk.

Parts of a house frame.Stud: Studs are the upright boards in a wall, typically spaced 16 inches apart in US construction.
Parts of a house frame.Joist: Joists are horizontal beams that support floors or ceilings, and the bounce underfoot depends on their size and span.
Parts of a house frame.Rafter: Rafters run from the ridge down to the walls, forming the slope of the roof and carrying its load downward.
Parts of a house frame.Beam: A beam carries a load across an opening, passing the weight to posts or walls at each end.
Parts of a house frame.Header: A header is the beam above a window or door, which carries the load around the opening so the frame holds.
Parts of a house frame.Truss: Roof trusses are built from triangles, and since triangles are rigid, a truss uses less wood than rafters would.
Parts of a house frame.Lintel: A lintel spans a door or window opening, and Stonehenge's horizontal capstones are famous ancient lintels.
Parts of a house frame.Sill plate: The sill plate is the wood bolted to the foundation, and the whole frame sits on it, which keeps it anchored.
Parts of a house frame.Ridge beam: The ridge beam is the horizontal timber along the roof's peak where the rafters meet, like a spine.
Parts of a house frame.Post: A post is an upright support that carries a beam or floor, as in a porch or open-plan room.
Parts of a house frame.Purlin: Purlins run horizontally across rafters or trusses to hold up the roof covering, and keep rafters from sagging.
Parts of a house frame.Shingle: Shingles cover the roof but aren't part of the frame. They sit over the hidden structure below.
Parts of a house frame.Drywall: Drywall is nailed onto the frame and isn't part of it. Sheetrock, the famous brand, appeared in 1916.
Parts of a house frame.Carpet: Carpet is a finishing layer laid on the floor after the structure is built, so it isn't part of the frame.
Parts of a house frame.Wallpaper: Wallpaper is decoration stuck on a finished wall long after the frame is up, so it isn't part of the skeleton.
Parts of a house frame.Window pane: A window pane sits inside a window frame, and is a fitted part, not a structural piece of the house skeleton.
Parts of a house frame.Doorknob: A doorknob is hardware fitted near the end of a build, long after the structure is complete.
Parts of a house frame.Curtain: Curtains hang over windows and can be changed any day, so they're décor and not part of the structure.
Parts of a house frame.Floor tile: Floor tile is a surface finish laid over the subfloor, long after the frame has been built and inspected.
Parts of a house frame.Paint: Paint is the last coat on a finished wall, so it comes long after the frame, and is not structural.
Parts of a house frame.Grout: Grout fills the joints between tiles, so it belongs to the finishing stage, not the structure.
Parts of a house frame.Light switch: A light switch is fitted into the wall after the frame is up, along with the rest of the wiring finishes.
Parts of a house frame.Faucet: A faucet is a plumbing fixture, fitted long after the frame is standing, and isn't structural.
Parts of a house frame.Doormat: A doormat is a floor item at the door, a small comfort with no role in holding up the house.

Video games released before 1990.Pac-Man: Released in 1980, it was reportedly inspired by a pizza missing a slice. It became the highest-grossing arcade game of its era.
Video games released before 1990.Tetris: Created in 1984 by Soviet programmer Alexey Pajitnov, it was later bundled with the Game Boy in 1989 and became a global phenomenon.
Released in 1985 on the NES, it helped revive the video game industry after the 1983 crash and remains among the best-selling games ever.
Video games released before 1990.The Legend of Zelda: Debuted in Japan in 1986, and its gold cartridge included a battery so players could save progress, which was novel at the time.
Video games released before 1990.Pong: Atari's 1972 table-tennis game, designed by Allan Alcorn as a training exercise, became the first commercially successful video game.
Video games released before 1990.Space Invaders: Taito's 1978 hit was a Japanese craze, and the aliens speed up as you shoot them because fewer sprites meant a faster-running game.
Video games released before 1990.Donkey Kong: Released in 1981, it introduced Mario, then called Jumpman. Shigeru Miyamoto designed it, and 'Donkey' was meant to suggest stubborn.
Video games released before 1990.Metroid: The 1986 original revealed, if you finished quickly, that its armored hero Samus was a woman, a rare twist for games then.
Video games released before 1990.Mega Man: Capcom's 1987 platformer lets you steal your defeated bosses' powers. Its Japanese title is Rockman, a pun pairing rock and roll.
Video games released before 1990.Final Fantasy: Released in 1987, it was named because developer Square was near bankruptcy and expected it to be their last game. It spawned a giant series.
Video games released before 1990.Castlevania: This 1986 Konami game sends a whip-wielding Belmont into Dracula's castle. Its name blends 'castle' and 'Transylvania'.
Video games released before 1990.Frogger: Konami's 1981 arcade game has you guide a frog across traffic and a river. It became one of the best-known arcade classics.
Video games released before 1990.Duck Hunt: The 1984 NES shooter used the Zapper light gun, which detected targets by briefly flashing them white on the screen. That dog is infamous for laughing.
Video games released before 1990.Sonic the Hedgehog: A trap: Sega's blue mascot arrived in 1991, just after the cutoff. He was created to rival Mario.
Video games released before 1990.Doom: id Software's 1993 shooter brought 3D gore to home PCs and popularized multiplayer deathmatch. Too late for this list.
Video games released before 1990.Minecraft: Markus Persson began it in 2009 and it's now the best-selling game of all time, so it's well after 1990.
Video games released before 1990.Mortal Kombat: Famed for its digitized actors and fatalities, it hit arcades in 1992 and helped spark the creation of the ESRB ratings board.
Video games released before 1990.Myst: A 1993 puzzle-adventure that sold millions and helped make CD-ROM drives popular. It came out a few years too late for this list.
Video games released before 1990.Halo: It began as a Mac strategy game at Bungie before becoming Xbox's 2001 launch shooter. Well after 1990.
Video games released before 1990.Super Mario 64: Its 1996 launch defined 3D platforming and showed how analog control sticks could work. Over six years too late.
Video games released before 1990.Crash Bandicoot: Naughty Dog's marsupial mascot arrived on the PlayStation in 1996, designed as Sony's answer to Mario and Sonic.
Video games released before 1990.Tomb Raider: Lara Croft first explored ruins in 1996, becoming one of gaming's first lasting female protagonists. Too late for this list.
Video games released before 1990.The Sims: Will Wright's life simulator arrived in 2000 and became one of the best-selling PC game series ever.
Video games released before 1990.Half-Life: Valve's debut from 1998 won over critics with its story told without cutscenes. Much later than 1990.

Characters in Oliver Twist.Oliver: The orphan raised in a workhouse made literature's most famous request, "Please, sir, I want some more."
Characters in Oliver Twist.Fagin: Dickens's criminal mastermind runs a gang of child pickpockets, and the portrait was criticised as an antisemitic stereotype, which Dickens later softened.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Artful Dodger: His real name is Jack Dawkins; his nickname and slick patter have made him shorthand for a clever young rogue.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Bill Sikes: The violent burglar's dog, Bull's-eye, is almost as famous as he is, and the brutal murder of Nancy made him Dickens's most terrifying villain.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Nancy: Despite her life among thieves, she risks everything to protect Oliver, and she pays for it with her life.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Mr. Bumble: The pompous parish beadle who runs the workhouse gave English the word "bumbledom" for petty, officious bureaucracy.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Mr. Brownlow: The kindly gentleman who takes Oliver in after a pickpocketing mix-up turns out to have a link to Oliver's parents.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Noah Claypole: The charity boy who bullies Oliver at the undertaker's later joins Fagin's gang as a cowardly informer.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Monks: This sinister stranger, Oliver's secret half-brother, plots to keep him in crime because of a hidden inheritance.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Bull's-eye: Sikes's loyal, ill-treated dog follows him in flight after the murder and ends up giving his master away.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Charley Bates: The lighthearted young pickpocket is so horrified by Sikes's murder of Nancy that he reforms and goes straight.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Mr. Sowerberry: The undertaker who employs Oliver has him walk behind coffins, which gives him an oddly dramatic start to life.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Pip: The hero of Great Expectations belongs to a different Dickens novel, from 1861.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Estella: Miss Havisham's cold ward is from Great Expectations, not Oliver Twist.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Scrooge: Dickens's famous miser is from A Christmas Carol, another book entirely.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Tiny Tim: The sickly boy who says "God bless us, every one" is from A Christmas Carol.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Magwitch: The convict on the marshes belongs to Great Expectations, not Oliver Twist's London underworld.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Uriah Heep: This oily, falsely humble clerk is from David Copperfield, a novel Dickens loved dearly.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Mr. Micawber: The cheerfully insolvent optimist, based partly on Dickens's own father, is from David Copperfield.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Miss Havisham: The jilted bride in her rotting wedding dress belongs to Great Expectations.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Little Nell: The pure child heroine of The Old Curiosity Shop is another Dickens figure, not Oliver's.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Sydney Carton: The hero who gives his life in A Tale of Two Cities says it's "a far, far better thing" than he has ever done.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Mr. Pickwick: The kind, comic founder of the Pickwick Club made Dickens famous in 1836, a few years before Oliver.
Characters in Oliver Twist.Madame Defarge: The knitting revolutionary who stitches the names of the doomed into her scarf comes from A Tale of Two Cities.

Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Ernest Hemingway: Too injured from two plane crashes in Africa to attend in 1954, he sent a speech to be read at the ceremony.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.John Steinbeck: Won in 1962; The Grapes of Wrath had been banned and even burned in some places in the 1930s.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.William Faulkner: His 1949 speech said man "will not merely endure: he will prevail", and it's one of the most quoted Nobel speeches.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Toni Morrison: In 1993 she became the first Black woman to win the literature prize, and she wrote Beloved.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Bob Dylan: In 2016 he became the first musician to win it, and he gave his lecture later, which was typical of him.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Kazuo Ishiguro: Won in 2017; born in Nagasaki and raised in England, he wrote The Remains of the Day and Never Let Me Go.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Rudyard Kipling: At 41 he was the youngest winner ever, in 1907, and he wrote The Jungle Book, Kim and the poem If.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.T. S. Eliot: Won in 1948, and his playful Old Possum poems later became the hit musical Cats on stage and screen.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Samuel Beckett: Won in 1969; he wrote Waiting for Godot in French first, then translated it himself into English.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Albert Camus: Won in 1957 at only 44, the author of The Stranger, and he died in a car crash in 1960, aged 46.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Pablo Neruda: The Chilean poet won in 1971, and is known for Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair, among others.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Winston Churchill: Won in 1953 for his histories and oratory, not for peace, which surprises many people who know his wartime role.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Leo Tolstoy: Nominated but never won, and he's often cited as among the biggest omissions in the prize's history.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.James Joyce: Ulysses made him a giant of modernism, but he never won the Nobel Prize, and he died in 1941.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Mark Twain: He died in 1910 without ever winning, though the prize had begun only in 1901, so his time was short.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Virginia Woolf: She never won the Nobel Prize, and she died in 1941 in the middle of the Second World War.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Marcel Proust: In Search of Lost Time is a masterpiece, but he never won the prize, and he died in 1922 aged 51.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Franz Kafka: He died in 1924 with most of his work unpublished, so he never won, nor knew of his later fame.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Jorge Luis Borges: A perennial favorite who famously never won the prize, despite being passed over for decades.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Vladimir Nabokov: Lolita's author never won the Nobel, though he was a favorite among readers for many years.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Anton Chekhov: He died in 1904 without winning, though he's one of the most performed playwrights anywhere.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Henrik Ibsen: The Norwegian playwright never won, and he died in 1906, five years after the prize began.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Graham Greene: A perennial candidate who never won, despite writing The Quiet American and The Third Man.
Won the Nobel Prize in Literature.Émile Zola: Nominated in 1901 and 1902, but he never won, and he died in 1902, early in the prize's life.

Wizards and witches in fiction.Gandalf: Tolkien took the name from a list of dwarves in Norse myth, and in his lore Gandalf is an angelic spirit, not a human.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Merlin: In Welsh tradition he came from the bard Myrddin, and in some legends he's the son of a demon and a human woman.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Dumbledore: Rowling said the name is an old word for a bumblebee, because she pictured him humming to himself.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Saruman: Tolkien's white wizard goes by the name Saruman, which comes from an Old English word for skill or craft.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Radagast: Radagast the Brown lives in Mirkwood and loves animals, and rides a sleigh pulled by rabbits in the Hobbit films.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Rincewind: Terry Pratchett's cowardly failed wizard wears a hat marked 'Wizzard' and runs from almost everything.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Ged: The Earthsea hero is nicknamed Sparrowhawk, and his true name, Ged, is revealed only to close friends.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Glinda: In Baum's books Glinda rules the South, but the 1939 film made her the Good Witch of the North.
Wizards and witches in fiction.The White Witch: In The Magician's Nephew Jadis comes from the dying world of Charn, where she spoke a word that destroyed everyone.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Prospero: Shakespeare's The Tempest is thought to be his last solo-written play, and Prospero's 'Our revels now are ended' is its most famous speech.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Baba Yaga: In Slavic folklore she lives in a hut that walks on chicken legs and flies in a mortar.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Mildred Hubble: Jill Murphy's clumsy trainee witch appeared in 1974, more than 20 years before Harry Potter.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Aragorn: Aragorn is a ranger and the heir to Gondor's throne, a skilled swordsman and healer but with no spells.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Frodo: Frodo is a hobbit and Ring-bearer who gets through his quest on courage and has no magic of his own.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Legolas: Legolas is an elf and an expert archer in Tolkien's tale, with keen eyesight, but he casts no spells.
Wizards and witches in fiction.King Arthur: Arthur is the king Merlin advises; he's a warrior, not a wizard, though Excalibur is magic.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Lancelot: Lancelot was added to the Arthur legend by Chrétien de Troyes in the 12th century, as a knight, not a wizard.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Peter Pan: Peter flies with the help of fairy dust and happy thoughts, but he's a boy, not a wizard.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Tinker Bell: Tinker Bell is a fairy who speaks only in tinkling bell sounds; fairy magic is a different matter from wizardry.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Aslan: Aslan is Narnia's divine lion, the creator and king, not a wizard, though his deep magic is older than the witch's.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Dorothy: Dorothy kills two witches by accident in Oz, but she's an ordinary Kansas girl, not a witch herself.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Alice: Alice is an ordinary Victorian girl who tumbles into other worlds, and does no magic.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Captain Hook: Captain Hook is a pirate and the villain of Peter Pan, and his only magic is the ability to hold a grudge.
Wizards and witches in fiction.Robin Hood: Robin Hood is an outlaw archer of Sherwood Forest with no magic, though later tales gave him Maid Marian.

Aircraft makers.Boeing: Boeing started in Seattle in 1916 as a maker of seaplanes, and the 747 jumbo jet, introduced in 1970, was the first wide-body airliner.
Aircraft makers.Airbus: Airbus is a European consortium formed in 1970, and its A380 is the world's largest passenger airliner, with a double-deck design.
Aircraft makers.Cessna: Cessna's 172 Skyhawk is the most-produced aircraft in history, with over 44,000 built, and many pilots learn to fly in one.
Aircraft makers.Embraer: Embraer is Brazil's aircraft maker, and it's one of the world's leading makers of regional jets and was founded as a state company in 1969.
Aircraft makers.Bombardier: Bombardier began in Quebec building snowmobiles, which became the Ski-Doo, and later moved into rail and business jets.
Aircraft makers.Lockheed Martin: Lockheed Martin's famous Skunk Works built the U-2 and SR-71 Blackbird, and its F-35 fighter is among the most expensive weapons programs ever.
Aircraft makers.Northrop Grumman: Northrop Grumman builds the B-2 stealth bomber, which costs billions of dollars per aircraft and has a flying-wing shape.
Aircraft makers.Gulfstream: Gulfstream, based in Savannah, Georgia, builds luxury business jets, and some of its models can fly non-stop for more than 12 hours.
Aircraft makers.Piper: Piper made the Cub, a light plane that taught generations of pilots to fly and is among the most recognizable light aircraft ever.
Aircraft makers.Dassault: Dassault is French, and it builds Mirage and Rafale fighters as well as Falcon business jets.
Aircraft makers.Sikorsky: Igor Sikorsky, a Russian immigrant, flew the first mass-produced helicopter in the US, and his company is now part of Lockheed Martin.
Aircraft makers.Lufthansa: Lufthansa is Germany's flag carrier, an airline, not an aircraft maker; its crane logo has been used since 1918.
Aircraft makers.Ryanair: Ryanair is an Irish airline, not a plane builder, and it's famous for rock-bottom fares and one of the biggest by passenger numbers in Europe.
Aircraft makers.Emirates: Emirates is an airline from Dubai, not a maker, and it flies one of the world's largest fleets of A380 superjumbos.
Aircraft makers.Qantas: Qantas is Australia's flag carrier, and its name stands for Queensland and Northern Territory Aerial Services, from 1920.
Aircraft makers.Delta: Delta Air Lines began as a crop-dusting business in Louisiana in 1925, and it's an airline, not a plane builder.
Aircraft makers.KLM: KLM, founded in 1919, is the oldest airline still flying under its original name, but it flies planes built by others.
Aircraft makers.Heathrow: Heathrow is London's busiest airport, and it's a place that handles planes, not a company that builds them.
Aircraft makers.Expedia: Expedia is a travel booking website, so it sells flights but doesn't build any aircraft, and it started inside Microsoft in 1996.
Aircraft makers.Concorde: Concorde is an aircraft, not a company; it was built by British Aerospace and Aérospatiale and cruised at twice the speed of sound.
Aircraft makers.Hertz: Hertz is a car rental firm, and it's a travel brand for airport pickup, not an aircraft maker.
Aircraft makers.Jetstar: Jetstar is a budget airline owned by Qantas, so it flies aircraft instead of making them.
Aircraft makers.easyJet: easyJet is a British low-cost airline famous for its orange branding; it buys Airbus aircraft rather than making any.
Aircraft makers.Spitfire: The Spitfire is a famous British fighter plane from World War II, made by Supermarine; it's a plane, not a maker.

Places of worship.Church: Christian place of worship, and the word comes from Greek 'kyriakon', meaning 'of the Lord'.
Places of worship.Mosque: The Muslim place of worship, and the word comes from the Arabic 'masjid', meaning a place of prostration.
Places of worship.Synagogue: A Jewish house of worship and study, and the word comes from Greek for 'assembly'.
Places of worship.Temple: A broad term for Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh and other houses of worship, and the Temple of Heaven in Beijing is one of the largest.
Places of worship.Cathedral: The seat of a bishop, and the word comes from 'cathedra', the Latin for his chair, so a cathedral is defined by a chair.
Places of worship.Chapel: A small place of worship, and the word comes from the cloak (cappella) of St. Martin, kept in a shrine.
Places of worship.Abbey: A monastery or convent ruled by an abbot or abbess, and Westminster Abbey is a coronation church, not a monastery now.
Places of worship.Basilica: The word comes from a Roman public hall, which Christians adopted as a church, and St. Peter's is the most famous.
Places of worship.Gurdwara: The Sikh house of worship, which has a free community kitchen called langar that serves anyone who comes.
Places of worship.Shrine: A holy place devoted to a deity or saint, and Japan's Shinto shrines are marked by torii gates.
Places of worship.Minster: An English word for a major church, originally for a monastery, as in York Minster, among the biggest Gothic cathedrals in Northern Europe.
Places of worship.Mausoleum: A tomb building, and the word comes from Mausolus' tomb at Halicarnassus, so it's for the dead, not for worship.
Places of worship.Castle: It's a fortified home, and its chapel may hold prayers, but it isn't a place of worship itself.
Places of worship.Palace: A royal residence, and it can include a chapel but isn't a house of worship.
Places of worship.Fortress: A military stronghold and though ones like Mont Saint-Michel have abbeys, it's defense that defines it.
Places of worship.Lighthouse: A coastal beacon for ships, and it's not for worship.
Places of worship.Observatory: A place to study stars, though ancient ones like Stonehenge may have had both roles, and it isn't worship.
Places of worship.Museum: A place to see artifacts, and the word comes from Greek for a place dedicated to the Muses.
Places of worship.Courthouse: Where trials are held, so it's civic rather than sacred, though many old courthouses borrowed temple-style columns and domes to look dignified.
Places of worship.Library: A place of books and study, which isn't a place of worship.
Places of worship.Bunker: A fortified underground shelter, so no worship.
Places of worship.Pyramid: Egyptian ones are tombs, not temples, though temples stood alongside them.
Places of worship.Colosseum: Rome's great arena, home to gladiator games and not a place of worship.
Places of worship.Barracks: Soldiers' housing, with no worship role.

Types of home people live in.Bungalow: The word comes from the Hindi bangla, meaning of Bengal, and the low houses were first built by British colonists in India.
Types of home people live in.Cottage: A cottage was originally the home of a farm laborer, and today the word suggests something quaint, thatched and cozy.
Types of home people live in.Igloo: True igloos are built from blocks of packed snow, and Inuit hunters used them mainly as temporary shelters during winter trips.
Types of home people live in.Mansion: The word comes from Latin for a staying place, and a mansion today usually means a very large and grand house.
Types of home people live in.Chalet: Chalets began as herders' huts in the Alps, and their wide, sloping roofs help snow slide off safely.
Types of home people live in.Villa: In ancient Rome a villa was a country estate, and Roman ones often had underfloor heating and elaborate mosaics.
Types of home people live in.Cabin: Log cabins reached North America with Swedish and Finnish settlers in the 1600s, and they were quick to build with simple tools.
Types of home people live in.Teepee: Plains peoples made tepees from buffalo hides stretched over poles, and the smoke flaps at the top could be adjusted to the wind.
Types of home people live in.Yurt: A yurt is a round felt tent used by Central Asian nomads, and it can be taken down and packed onto camels in a few hours.
Types of home people live in.Hut: Huts are among the simplest homes, and across the world they can be built from mud, thatch or branches in a matter of days.
Types of home people live in.Townhouse: A townhouse shares walls with its neighbors, and in London the elegant terraces of Georgian times shaped the whole city.
Types of home people live in.Duplex: A duplex holds two separate homes in one building, and the word is Latin for twofold.
Types of home people live in.Houseboat: In Srinagar, India, houseboats on Dal Lake are intricately carved wooden homes that have served as lodgings for visitors for generations.
Types of home people live in.Silo: A silo stores grain or fodder, though some silos have been converted into trendy homes, so it isn't typically a place to live.
Types of home people live in.Garage: A garage shelters cars, and the word comes from the French verb garer, which means to shelter or dock.
Types of home people live in.Shed: Sheds store tools, and a backyard shed with a bed isn't legal housing in many places despite the rise of tiny-home fashion.
Types of home people live in.Warehouse: Warehouses hold goods, though many old ones have been turned into loft apartments, so the building isn't usually a home.
Types of home people live in.Factory: Factories make goods, and the first modern ones appeared in 18th-century Britain, but nobody typically lives in them.
Types of home people live in.Kiosk: Kiosk comes from a Turkish word for a garden pavilion, and today it's a tiny stand for selling papers or snacks.
Types of home people live in.Gazebo: Gazebos are open garden structures for shade, and the word may be a joke combining the Latin gaze and the future ending of I shall.
Types of home people live in.Pavilion: Pavilion comes from Latin for butterfly, because a billowing tent resembled one, and it houses events, not families.
Types of home people live in.Stadium: Stadium comes from the Greek stadion, a footrace length of about 180 meters, and nobody lives inside one.
Types of home people live in.Pergola: Pergolas are open frames covered in climbing plants, and they offer shade for patios but no walls or roof to live under.
Types of home people live in.Greenhouse: Greenhouses trap warmth for plants, and the first modern ones appeared in Europe in the 1600s to grow oranges in cold climates.

Things with handlebars.Bicycle: Karl von Drais's 1817 'running machine', the ancestor of the bicycle, was already steered with a handlebar, though it had no pedals.
Things with handlebars.Motorcycle: Gottlieb Daimler's 1885 wooden Reitwagen is generally counted as the first motorcycle, steered with a simple handlebar.
Things with handlebars.Scooter: Vespa means 'wasp' in Italian, a name given to the 1946 scooter for its buzzing engine and narrow waist.
Things with handlebars.Moped: The word moped blends 'motor' and 'pedal', and early ones really could be pedaled when the little engine failed.
Things with handlebars.Jet ski: Jet Ski is actually Kawasaki's trademark, though people use it for every personal watercraft, which are steered with handlebars.
Things with handlebars.Snowmobile: Canadian inventor Joseph-Armand Bombardier developed practical snowmobiles from the 1930s, and the handlebars steer the front skis.
Things with handlebars.Quad bike: Early three-wheeled all-terrain vehicles were pulled from the US market in 1988 over safety worries, which is why four wheels became the norm.
Things with handlebars.Segway: The Segway's owner, Jimi Heselden, died in 2010 when he rode one off a cliff. Production of the original ended in 2020.
Things with handlebars.Exercise bike: Spinning classes, built around indoor bikes, were launched in the 1990s by cyclist Johnny Goldberg, known as Johnny G.
Things with handlebars.Tricycle: Queen Victoria reportedly owned two tricycles, and adult trikes were popular in the 1880s with riders who wanted stability.
Things with handlebars.Dirt bike: Dirt bikes descend from British 'scrambles' races of the 1920s, which evolved into motocross.
Things with handlebars.Car: Cars use a steering wheel, which replaced the tiller-style handles of the earliest automobiles.
Things with handlebars.Bus: A bus uses a large steering wheel, since a handlebar couldn't give enough leverage on a big vehicle.
Things with handlebars.Skateboard: A skateboard has no handlebar. Riders steer by leaning, and the tilt turns the trucks.
Things with handlebars.Unicycle: Most unicycles have no handlebars, though some mountain models add a handle for balance.
Things with handlebars.Canoe: A canoe is steered by paddle strokes, and there's nothing to hold but the paddle.
Things with handlebars.Kayak: A kayak is moved and steered with a double-bladed paddle, so there are no handlebars.
Things with handlebars.Hot air balloon: A hot air balloon rises by heating the air, and its pilot steers only by finding winds at different altitudes.
Things with handlebars.Train: A train is steered by the rails, so no handlebars are needed, though the driver has a throttle and a brake handle.
Things with handlebars.Rollerblades: Rollerblades are steered by the skater's leaning, so no handlebars are used.
Things with handlebars.Surfboard: Surfers steer by shifting weight on the board, and there's nothing to hold but the water.
Things with handlebars.Tank: A tank is steered with levers or a wheel that brake one track, and some tanks use a handlebar-like yoke.
Things with handlebars.Helicopter: A helicopter pilot uses a cyclic stick and collective lever, not handlebars, to control the aircraft.
Things with handlebars.Glider: A glider is steered with a stick and rudder pedals, and has no engine to need handlebars.

Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Chariot: Rome's Circus Maximus could hold well over 100,000 people for chariot races, which were wildly popular events.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Stagecoach: A stagecoach traveled in 'stages' between stations where fresh horses were swapped, which is how it got its name.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Carriage: Britain's Gold State Coach, built in 1760, has carried every monarch to coronation since 1831, and takes a team of eight horses.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Hansom cab: The hansom cab was patented in 1834 by Joseph Hansom, an architect who also designed Birmingham Town Hall.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Dog sled: In 1925, relays of dog sled teams carried diphtheria antitoxin to Nome, Alaska, in about five days, and the lead dog Balto became famous.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Covered wagon: Pioneers often pulled covered wagons with oxen rather than horses, and the white-topped wagons were nicknamed prairie schooners.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Oxcart: Painted oxcarts are a national symbol of Costa Rica, and the tradition is on UNESCO's heritage list.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Sleigh: Sleigh bells were added so silent sleighs wouldn't surprise pedestrians, and 'Jingle Bells' was originally a Thanksgiving song.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Pumpkin coach: In Perrault's 1697 Cinderella, the fairy godmother turns a pumpkin into a coach, and mice into horses.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Rickshaw: A rickshaw is pulled by a person, not an animal. The Japanese name 'jinrikisha' literally means human-powered vehicle.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Pedicab: A pedicab is pedaled by a cyclist, so people, not animals, provide the power.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Tuk-tuk: A tuk-tuk runs on a small motor, so it isn't animal-drawn.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Wheelbarrow: Chinese inventors were using wheelbarrows roughly 2,000 years ago, and they are pushed by hand.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Toboggan: A toboggan slides down a snowy hill by gravity alone, with no animals needed.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Bobsled: A bobsled races down ice by gravity, and the fastest runs top 130 km/h.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Handcar: A handcar rolls on railways, powered by people pumping a lever, not animals.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Pram: A pram is pushed by a parent, so no animals pull it.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Skateboard: A skateboard is pushed by foot, and has no animals involved.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Scooter: A scooter is kicked along by foot or driven by a small motor, and no animals pull it.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Segway: A Segway balances itself with gyroscopes and electric motors, so it is neither animal- nor pedal-driven.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Shopping cart: The shopping cart was invented in 1937 by Sylvan Goldman in Oklahoma City, and pushed by shoppers.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Go-kart: A go-kart is small and motor-driven, so no animals need apply.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Luge: A luge is ridden feet-first down ice tracks by gravity, with speeds over 140 km/h.
Vehicles traditionally pulled by animals.Soapbox car: A soapbox car rolls downhill under gravity, built by kids and racers, with no animals pulling it.

Things at a ski resort.Ski lift: The first ski lift in the Alps appeared in the 1930s, and today resorts lift thousands of skiers every hour on the busiest lines.
Things at a ski resort.Chairlift: The chairlift was first built at Sun Valley, Idaho, in 1936, inspired by the hoists that loaded bananas onto ships.
Things at a ski resort.Gondola: Resort gondolas are enclosed cable cabins that keep skiers warm; the name borrows from Venice's boats, which they resemble.
Things at a ski resort.Chalet: Chalet comes from Swiss French and meant a herdsman's hut before becoming a symbol of alpine holidays.
Things at a ski resort.Piste: Piste is French for "track"; in Europe, runs are graded green, blue, red and black, with black the hardest.
Things at a ski resort.Snowcat: Snowcats are tracked machines that groom pistes overnight, so the snow is smooth by morning.
Things at a ski resort.Moguls: Moguls are the bumps that form where skiers turn; freestyle mogul skiing became an Olympic medal event in 1992.
Things at a ski resort.T-bar: The T-bar pulls two skiers uphill on their skis, by a bar shaped like an upside-down T.
Things at a ski resort.Ski patrol: Ski patrollers rescue injured skiers, and also trigger controlled avalanches with explosives to make the slopes safe.
Things at a ski resort.Half-pipe: Half-pipe riding comes from skateboarding and made its Olympic snowboarding debut at the 1998 Nagano Games.
Things at a ski resort.Snow cannon: Snow cannons spray water as a fine mist that freezes into snow, but only when it's cold enough, usually below about minus two degrees.
Things at a ski resort.Lifeguard tower: Lifeguard towers watch over swimmers at the beach, so they'd be pointless on snow.
Things at a ski resort.Surfboard: Surfing began in Polynesia centuries ago; it's all waves, and the opposite of a ski slope.
Things at a ski resort.Sandcastle: A sandcastle needs damp sand; the biggest ever built stood over 20 metres high.
Things at a ski resort.Beach hut: Beach huts are common on British seafronts, and some of them sell for six figures.
Things at a ski resort.Pier: A pier is a platform stretching out over the sea, as at Brighton or Santa Monica.
Things at a ski resort.Palm tree: Palms grow in warm climates, though a few hardy species tolerate occasional frost; they don't grow on ski slopes.
Things at a ski resort.Snorkel: The snorkel lets divers breathe at the surface; ironically, ski resorts rent equipment of a different type, such as goggles.
Things at a ski resort.Cactus: Cacti live in deserts, mostly in the Americas, and store water in their thick stems; skiing isn't their thing.
Things at a ski resort.Jet ski: The jet ski is a brand name that became a generic term; it is a water craft and is no use on snow.
Things at a ski resort.Coral: Coral reefs grow in warm shallow seas, and cover less than one percent of the ocean floor.
Things at a ski resort.Flip-flops: Flip-flops date back thousands of years, as ancient Egyptians wore a similar sandal made of papyrus.
Things at a ski resort.Seashell: Seashells are the hard homes of molluscs; they wash up on beaches, not on ski slopes.
Things at a ski resort.Coconut: A coconut is not technically a nut, and coconuts can float for thousands of kilometres across the ocean.

Famous architects.Frank Lloyd Wright: Fallingwater, his house built over a waterfall in Pennsylvania, is often called the best American building ever.
Famous architects.Zaha Hadid: In 2004 she became the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize, and her flowing, curved buildings defied straight lines.
Famous architects.Antoni Gaudí: Gaudí's Sagrada Família in Barcelona has been under construction since 1882 and is due to be completed around 2026.
Famous architects.Le Corbusier: He called a house 'a machine for living in', and his Swiss-born name was really Charles-Édouard Jeanneret.
Famous architects.Frank Gehry: Gehry's titanium-clad Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, opened in 1997, revived the city and coined the 'Bilbao effect'.
Famous architects.I. M. Pei: Pei designed the glass pyramid at the Louvre in Paris, controversial when it opened in 1989 but now iconic.
Famous architects.Norman Foster: Foster designed the 'Gherkin' tower in London, and the glass dome of the Reichstag in Berlin.
Famous architects.Christopher Wren: After the Great Fire of 1666, Wren rebuilt dozens of London churches and designed St Paul's Cathedral.
Famous architects.Mies van der Rohe: His motto 'less is more' shaped glass-and-steel skyscrapers, and he led the Bauhaus school in its last years.
Famous architects.Renzo Piano: Piano co-designed the Pompidou Centre in Paris with its pipes on the outside, and later London's Shard.
Famous architects.Oscar Niemeyer: Brazil's Niemeyer designed most of the modernist capital Brasília, a city built from scratch in the 1950s.
Famous architects.Pablo Picasso: Picasso was a painter and sculptor, famous for Cubism and Guernica, not for designing buildings.
Famous architects.Claude Monet: Monet's blurry water lily paintings and his sunrise canvas gave Impressionism its name, but he was a painter.
Famous architects.Salvador Dalí: Dalí painted melting clocks in The Persistence of Memory, making him a surrealist painter, not an architect.
Famous architects.Auguste Rodin: Rodin sculpted The Thinker, and some of his work stood on buildings, but he was a sculptor.
Famous architects.Andy Warhol: Warhol made Campbell's soup can prints and celebrity portraits, a Pop Art painter, not an architect.
Famous architects.Vincent van Gogh: Van Gogh sold almost nothing in life but painted about 900 paintings, none for buildings.
Famous architects.Frida Kahlo: Kahlo is known for vivid self-portraits, and her blue house in Mexico City is now a museum, but she was a painter.
Famous architects.Banksy: Anonymous street artist Banksy is famous for stencil graffiti, and a painting shredded itself right after selling in 2018.
Famous architects.Henri Matisse: Matisse led the Fauves with bold color and later made paper cut-outs; he also designed a chapel in Vence, France.
Famous architects.Georgia O'Keeffe: O'Keeffe painted giant flowers and desert bones of New Mexico, and was a painter, not an architect.
Famous architects.Rembrandt: Rembrandt was a Dutch master of light and shadow, famous for The Night Watch, and not an architect.
Famous architects.Jackson Pollock: Pollock dripped paint across canvases laid on the floor, and was an abstract painter, not a builder.
Famous architects.Edvard Munch: Munch's The Scream exists in several versions, one stolen from Oslo in 2004, and he was a painter.

Add 'plane' to make a word.Sail: A sailplane is a glider with long thin wings built for soaring.
Add 'plane' to make a word.Ski: A ski plane lands on snow with skids instead of wheels.
Add 'plane' to make a word.Aqua: An aquaplane is a board towed behind a speedboat, which preceded the waterski.
Add 'plane' to make a word.Tail: The tailplane is the small horizontal wing at the back that keeps a plane level.
Add 'plane' to make a word.Space: A spaceplane flies like a plane but reaches space, like the Space Shuttle, which glided in to land.
